subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CUT IN TAXATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Federal government taxation is killing business and pounding the life out of the people. One utility company which paid a total federal tax of $8 million in 1980 was required to pay $64 million in 1981, or eight times as much, even though its revenue was only three quarters of the 1980 revenue. This increase was due to the excise tax and the Canadian ownership tax. These taxes are passed on to the people, including the aged, the poor and the crippled. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper):
That this House urge the government in the name of humanity and compassion to cut these taxes before we have a tax revolution in this country.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the information branch of the Commissioner of Official Languages recently published a map supposedly depicting the languages of the world. The map is apparently intended as a teaching aid for students from the age of 13 to 17 years. The map pointedly omits any reference to the Ukrainian language. There are over 600,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent in this country who have contributed their language and their traditions to enhance the cultural mosaic of Canada. The publication of this map by the government is an insult to each and every one of them. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn):
That this House direct the Commissioner of Official Languages to withdraw this offensive map immediately and prepare a proper one which recognizes the Ukrainian language as one of the world's languages.

Madam Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has been talking about a national beef program of one sort or another for over a year. In the meantime, because of the lack of any effective national program, every beef producing province has announced assistance to the beef industry which significantly varies from province to province. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Today the Canadian dollar fell to its lowest level since the depths of the depression 50 years ago, before the Bank of Canada stepped in to support it. This alarming drop reflects the conviction of investors that the government will again introduce the wrong economic policy at the wrong time and take steps to devalue the dollar or bring on exchange controls. Will the Prime Minister commit to this House, on the basis of whatever credibility his government still possesses, that the government is not planning to devalue the dollar or impose exchange controls, now or in the foreseeable future?

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS MADE BY UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR TO CANADA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 have a question for the Prime Minister. The internationally accepted role of an ambassador is that an envoy should not interfere in the host country's politics by speaking out publicly on matters which are to be resolved domestically. Considering that the United States ambassador to Canada has once again violated this principle, this time by asserting, on the one hand, that Canadians spend too much on social programs and, on the other hand, by asserting publicly that we should not strengthen our FIR A legislation, what action does the Government of Canada propose to take to ensure that this does not happen again?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS MADE BY UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR TO CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member has not stated the international rule exactly. It is that ambassadors are expected to represent their countries in another country and to speak on issues in that country which affect their own country's interests and policies. As I am sure all hon. members of the House would wish, we give a fairly wide latitude to that rule, just as we would expect other countries to do so in the case of our ambassadors.
I would admit what the hon. gentleman says, that there are some instances which, from time to time, could be considered borderline. In those cases, by and large, I think it is better that those be dealt with, as long as they are borderline, by the normal political and free speech process of this country, so that members like the Minister of National Defence or other members of this House can publicly answer things which are publicly said. It seems to me that that is in the best tradition of Canadian democracy.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the responsibility today to present a petition signed by some 994 residents of my constituency of Elgin. These citizens, by way of this petition, are vigorously demonstrating their strong and united opposition to the private member's bill, C-451, and consider its purpose to be a serious infringement on their rights as law-abiding Canadian gun owners.
I believe the record should show that Bill C-451 is not a government bill and has not received second reading, in spite of what the petition indicates.
I fully support the views of the petitioners and indeed, judging from the conversations and correspondence that I have had with the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), the changes sought in Bill C-451 will indeed not become law.

Do grain box cars or grain hopper cars on CN rail lines travel to Thunder Bay via Vancouver and Peace River and, if so (a) how frequently and what is the reason for the error (b) is the cost absorbed by the railway company or by the farmers directly (c) is CNR taking measures to alleviate the problem and, if so, what measures?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: GRAIN BOXCAR NO. CN-422258
speechtext:
The management of the Canadian National Railways and Transport Canada advise as follows:
1.	On November 20, 1981, the Alberta Wheat Pool agent at Rosalind, Alberta, gave "telephone release" to CN's Edmonton Carload Centre for three carloads, including CN-422258, loaded with oats, (a) Yes. (b) The carload travelled from Vancouver to Athabasca and then to Thunder Bay.
2.	(a) Rarely. In this instance an error was made in recording the information given by the pool agent in the "telephone release", and as a result, the billing details fed into CN's computer system recorded the destination for CN-422258 as Vancouver. Upon arrival there, it was sent to the Lynn Creek Yard to await placement to a terminal elevator; subsequently, the loaded car was diverted to Vancouver's Thornton Yard and returned to Edmonton's Calder Yard where the staff, being unaware the car had not been unloaded, sent it to Athabasca, Alberta. At that point it was found to be still under load and was returned to Edmonton. Identification and destination were established and the car was forwarded to Thunder Bay.
(b)	The cost of the extra transportation was absorbed by Canadian National in this case.
(c)	Canadian National is continually striving for the elimination of this type of error.
3.	The Canadian Wheat Board has access to the railway car training computers and the Grain Transportation Authority also keeps a close watch on car movements. It should not be forgotten that last crop year 233,686 cars were unloaded at Thunder Bay while 150,059 were unloaded on the west coast. The vast majority of these cars were moved to terminal position with dispatch.

speechtext:
that Bill C-112, to amend the statute law relating to certain taxes, be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.
He said: Madam Speaker, yesterday hon. members had an opportunity to discuss a borrowing authority bill, and on that occasion I explained that we were resuming second reading on the same subject because the previous borrowing authority bill, which also covered, in its second part, a number of amendments to the Excise Tax Act and in its third part, the legislation on natural gas and oil revenue taxes, had been split, following discussions between the government, opposition and New Democratic House leaders and the finance and energy critics, to provide a format for debate on borrowing authority and fiscal measures that was more appropriate in the opinion of hon. members. I also explained that, in addition to splitting the bill in two and thus providing for separate debates, this agreement also provided a time limit for debate in the House, in Committee of the Whole or in the standing committee, depending on the bill. I explained to the House that I would restrict my comments so as to enable the largest possible number of members with an interest in this issue, both on this side and on the other side of the House, to speak to this bill.
During the debate on the previous bill, which in its second and third parts covered the subject of the present bill, hon. members complained that the government had failed to explain why the bill raised the ceiling on the natural gas tax from 70 cents to $4.00 per gigajoule. I shall briefly give some of our reasons for wanting to regulate the tax in this way.
At the present time, the Excise Tax Act provides for a set schedule of tax increases, according to which the tax increased from 28 cents on November 1, 1980, to 56 cents on January 1, 1982, and will increase to 70 cents on January 1, 1983. The schedule was established on the basis of assumptions relating to the policies and prices set in the National Energy Program which, the House will recall, was announced in October, 1980. According to this policy, the tax will apply to both domestic and export sales, according to a proposal in the National Energy Program published in October, 1980. Hon. members will recall that the province of Alberta objected to the price schedule set in the National Energy Program and objected very strenuously to the tax on natural gas exports. Following negotiations, it was agreed to increase domestic oil prices beyond the prices provided in the National Energy Program, and following this increase, to abolish the natural gas export
tax. Thus, a new mechanism had to be established for determining what the natural gas tax rate would be. The House will recall that the tax rate must be set in such a way that the ratio thus established between the price of natural gas and the price of oil in eastern Canada will promote the use of natural gas in eastern markets. This ratio is determined by the natural gas tax rate, the price and quantity of imported oil, the price paid to producers for domestic oil and natural gas, the Canadian ownership tax rate and the cost of transporting natural gas from Alberta to the eastern provinces.
Thus, we have a complex formula with a large number of variables. If the use of a specific formula of this kind were prescribed by law, the result would have been frequent rate variations, perhaps every two months or even more often. The companies that distribute natural gas to consumers raised the point that the time and money involved in implementing the rate changes, including the submission of applications to regulatory commissions, could, and certainly would create a number of problems. Therefore they requested a procedure for minimizing the administrative costs resulting from too frequent changes in this tax. By prescribing the rate of the tax through regulations, we shall have some flexibility and the margin of autonomy required to reduce the effect of shortterm mistakes in the variables underlying this complex formula which I described earlier.
A ceiling of $4 had been chosen as the maximum amount in a possible range of rates which would apply during the life of the energy agreement between Canada and Alberta. In view of the forecast increases in world oil prices and the expected reduction in natural gas transportation costs, it is possible, while not probable, that the tax could reach $4 per gigajoule by 1987. However, to meet the representations and the requests of certain hon. members, I undertake to introduce in committee of the whole an amendment to lower the ceiling from $4 to $3 per gigajoule. Moreover, I shall propose in the same amendment that this ceiling of $3 be phased in over a number of years for the period of the agreement. I believe that this amendment will meet the requests and the representations made during the debate on second reading. Of course, this does not meet all the representations made at that time, but it responds to a basic concern reflected by these representations.
The rate of tax proposed in this bill for the year 1982 is not much higher than the rate provided by existing legislation. In 1982, the tax will amount to 42 cents for January and 63 cents for the rest of the year, which gives an average of 61 cents over a 12-month period. This rate is only five cents higher than that prescribed by the existing legislation. I would also like to emphasize that the removal of the tax on natural gas exported from Alberta and British Columbia reflects the wish of this government to take into account the representations made by the producing provinces. Moreover, the fact that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has been able
May 13, 1982

to reach an agreement on so critical a subject as oil and gas prices demonstrates that the government, and particularly the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on behalf of the government, has shown a lot of flexibility and skill in his negotiations with the producing provinces.
In view of the objective which is to increase the share of the Canadian government in the revenues generated by oil and gas production, and especially of the emphasis placed on the need to obtain this increase by other means than an export tax, it has been necessary to increase other taxes collected from the industry, such as the oil and gas revenue tax. I would like to remind hon. members once again that the bill now under consideration simply implements the arrangements arrived at after months of intensive and skilful negotiations between the Government of Canada and the provinces, and which were finalized and officially endorsed in the agreements signed with the Premiers of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Mr. Speaker, through this bill, the House is asked to approve the agreements signed between the Government of Canada and those of the producing provinces.
Concerning the provisions for levying special taxes on profits derived from crude oil production, I would remind the House that all other producing countries insist that their government get a significant part of oil revenues. Britain, Norway, Mexico, the OPEC countries all levy heavy taxes on production. The United States are already levying a tax on windfall profits from old oil operations in order to tax extra profits on the production of oil that has long been discovered. This bill provides for the implementing of a tax on incremental oil revenues, in respect of revenues derived from the production of old oil. That tax is meant to achieve exactly the same purpose as the American tax I have just described.
I would remind the House that the financial situation of oil companies in Canada compares favourably with that of companies in most other oil-producting countries. Although a number of Canadian companies thought they would be better off if they invested money in oil operations in the United States, they now realize that involvement in the United States is not without any risks. The Canadian government here is generously encouraging Canadian corporations into finding new oil, through the many incentives to be found in the Canadian Energy Program. Sure enough, Mr. Speaker, the government is not unaware of the indebtedness of some companies, of the decline in world oil prices, and of the impact which capped oil and gas wells may have on the industry. 1 want to assure hon. members that the government and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) are closely monitoring that situation.
This bill introduces a resource deduction from the oil and natural gas revenue tax. As of January 1st, 1982, there is a 25 per cent deduction on production revenues, before deduction of any resource royalty payment. Such a provision was requested by the province of Alberta in order that the oil and gas revenue tax be levied at a later stage after extraction. The deduction structure was also designed to grant an extra incentive to
Taxation
operators who pay Crown royalties and transfer part of their production revenues to other persons in the form of royalties. Those royalties are not deducted from revenues on which the 25 per cent resource deduction will be based. Details of the resource deduction will be introduced in the oil and gas revenue tax regulations. Legislative authority to proceed this way is provided under Clause 19 of the legislation now before us.
Mr. Speaker, the bill also includes a number of lesser provisions that relate to the federal sales tax. I do not wish to take time to outline these provisions, since the hon. members who referred to them admitted that the amendments are of a rather technical nature. As I said in my opening remarks, an agreement was reached to expedite the legislation, and I hope that all the hon. members who wish to contribute to this debate will have an opportunity to do so. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I am limiting my remarks to the few minutes I have used up to outline the main aspects of the legislation and to confirm to the House the commitment to change both the ceiling and the implementation of national gas taxes and savings.

Mr. Speaker, I must say I was a little bit surprised to see the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) as opening speaker for the government on this legislation, given that the taxes imposed and legalized by this legislation represent the very heart of the National Energy Program in terms of the devastation it has wreaked upon this country.
Bill C-112 introduces three new monstrously huge federal taxes extracted from the oil industry and the consumers of this country. They are monstrous taxes; not minor, not insignificant, but monstrous. They are so monstrous as to have caused the decimation of the oil and gas industry in this country. Prior to the introduction of the National Energy Program, that industry was one of the most vital and healthy in this country. It provided hundreds of thousands of jobs and earned the country enormous amounts of income. In general, it provided an engine for growth in the economy from coast to coast.
Prior to the National Energy Program and these taxes being introduced, the energy industries in Canada were looked upon with envy by other countries. They were looked upon by economic groups such as the Economic Council of Canada as our ace in the hole, the one thing Canada had going for it that would give us a chance in the eighties. It was to make this country purr in the eighties. It could have generated the hundreds of thousands of jobs that are necessary for our population. This is what the energy industry could have been, would have been and was predicted to be in the eighties.
If it had not been for the National Energy Program as exemplified by these taxes, we would not be facing the interest

May 13, 1982
Taxation
rates we face today; they would be two or three points less. We would not be facing nearly the number of unemployed we now have. At least 100,000 more Canadians would be employed. Instead of looking at a depression which more and more people are seeing for the future, we would be looking at a rosy future indeed.
That is what this bill exemplifies-taking away the future of Canada as we go into the eighties. It is a massive, horrendous tax grab that has devastated the industry. It has driven many into bankruptcy, driven many out of the country, driven a lot to the brink of bankruptcy and caused havoc. That is the consequence of the taxes levied by this bill which are part of a so-called National Energy Program. There is nothing national about it if one considers the energy sectors of this country, the oil and gas producing sectors in western Canada, as being a part of this nation.
This bill is a massive tax grab as a result of analysis done by brilliant people working for the minister at Tunney's Pasture. They prepared for him and a new cabinet an analysis of the energy sector in Canada. I saw that analysis. They projected what was going to happen. They projected what was happening in terms of ownership, what was happening in terms of activity. They projected an absolutely devastating scenario unless the government acted. They projected huge revenue flows into the oil and gas sector in western Canada. Their projects were such that, if they were right, something would indeed have to be done because the country would have been destabilized as a result of this massive transfer of wealth into a very small area, namely, the province of Alberta.
Based on these projections by those geniuses in Tunney's Pasture, they produced the National Energy Program. It was the answer to a hypothetical, totally false, totally inaccurate description of the future. It makes one wonder when there will be a recognition of all of this cabinet secrecy, all of this notion that no one should know what the government is doing until it is finally announced, and when we are going to address that problem. Anyone who had any knowledge whatsoever of the energy sector could have destroyed those analyses which were prepared by the officials for the minister. You did not have to be particularly brilliant. All you had to have was a little bit of knowledge of the real world, in terms of the energy industry, to know that the projections made by those officials were wholly inaccurate.
Of course, the system which is designed by the bureaucrats for the protection of the bureaucrats does not allow that. So they sit there, they put together a scenario, and they convince the minister, who knows no more than they about what is going on in that part of the country. That is not intended to be demeaning in any way, that is the reality. He would not know any more about energy than I know about fishing. I do not happen to live in a fishing area and so have not been exposed to the fishing industry. So the minister did not know the energy industry, he is advised by officials who do not know the energy industry, on an analysis that is totally out of whack
with reality, and the consequences of that are the National Energy Program, which destroys the industry.

speechtext:
I want to deal with the natural gas and gas liquids tax. Mr. Speaker, there is another technique that governments use for disguishing what they are really doing. When you talk about taxes to the ordinary citizen, the citizen assumes that you are talking about income tax and says that everyone should pay income tax and contribute to the upkeep of the government. He looks at analyses of income tax paid by Canadian industry and says they are not paying very much tax, that they can afford to pay more. But what the citizens fail to realize is how many new taxes the government has invented. Those new taxes do not mean very much to the public; they cannot be concerned about them when they do not know about them. We have the natural gas and gas liquids tax, the NGGLT, the PGRT, the petroleum gas revenue tax, the oil warranty, the incremental oil revenue tax, the COC, the Canadian ownership charge, the PCC, the petroleum compensation charge and, of course, there is excise tax and sales tax on top of that. There are about seven or eight different taxes, the sum total of which is a horrendous tax load on one sector. How come? That sector happens to be in an area of the country which does not have that much population; therefore they are not able to express through the ballot box their indignation in a way to cause the government and the bureaucrats harm.
Yesterday in committee the member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre) said he wished he had some oil wells in his riding, and I had to say "Amen, me too!" Boy, I wish there were some oil wells in Pontiac, in Montreal and in Quebec and Toronto. I wish there were oil wells all over central Canada, because that is the only way we would ever get a national Canadian energy policy. That is the only way we will get one until the system is changed.
In regard to this natural gas and gas liquids tax, there is an interesting little history on how that one came about. Just prior to introducing the national energy policy, which was part of the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in October, 1980, the government were threatening to put an export tax on natural gas. That was objected to quite strenuously by the province of British Columbia in particular and also by the province of Alberta. There was a lot of lobbying and agitation on that matter, so the government was feeling the heat. When the Minister of Finance read his budget speech, he said, right in the budget speech: "In response to the representations, there will be no export tax on gas". And because they had a lock up and were able to control the media, that is what went out on national television-"No export tax on natural gas". That is what the propaganda masters had told the television and radio people who were at the lock up. The very next line in the speech said: "There will be a charge on gas sold to United States customers." That was the very next
May 13, 1982

line-a charge on gas sold to U.S. customers. If that is not an export tax, what is it?
Mr. Speaker, I am not allowed to say that is a lie; I am not allowed to say the author of that is a liar. But what is it, Mr. Speaker? It certainly is not true?
Then the province of Alberta took the federal government to court and said this charge on gas sold to U.S. customers is in violation of the Constitution of Canada. The lawyer representing the federal government, Mr. William Code, said the federal government had the authority to put on an export tax. The judges said: "Well, the Minister of Finance said it is not an export tax." Mr. Code replied: "Well, in reality it is an export tax." So the government had to admit in court that what the Minister of Finance had said to this, the highest court in the land, was not true. The Minister of Finance who said there would be no export tax was deceiving this House and the country when he made that statement, and that is what the lawyer for the government had to admit in a courthouse in Alberta. The court ruled, five to nothing, that that export tax was unconstitutional.
So the negotiations carry on. The federal government now has to negotiate. They lost in court so they have to negotiate. They negotiated with the province of Alberta and in the negotiations said: "Yes, we are going to have an export tax on natural gas, but the export tax will be zero rated."

I am not commenting on the merits of the argument or the lack of them, other than to state the fact that the Supreme Court of Alberta ruled, five to nothing, against the federal government.

What we have in this bill is an export tax, zero rated. There is no export tax; there is a charge on gas sold to U.S. consumers. There is an export tax but it is zero rated. If that is not Orwellian 1984 double-speak, I do not know what is. It is no wonder the public does not know what is going on when that kind of language is used.
How much is involved for this fiscal year? In this current fiscal year that tax will bring in $1,505 billion, a very large amount. I do not want to prejudice court cases, but it seems that the only way to get things done in this country nowadays is to go to court because this institution, the highest court in the land, does not work.
There is another case going on respecting the NGGLT between the federal government and the city of Medicine Hat. The city of Medicine Hat is suing the federal government because this natural gas and gas liquids tax has caused utility bills in the city of Medicine Hat to double. The cost of heating a home in Medicine Hat has doubled as a result of this tax. Rudyard Kipling said, "They have all hell for a basement." In Medicine Hat natural gas is literally underneath the people's houses. It is just a few feet below. It is available everywhere in the vicinity of Medicine Hat. For 100 years people there have heated their homes with natural gas literally taken right out of their basements, and now they are facing horrendous increased costs.
What is really ridiculous is that it is now more expensive to use natural gas for various agriculture purposes-operating sprinkler systems in irrigation areas and so forth-than it is to use diesel fuel. Diesel fuel is refined. In the case of Medicine Hat I think it has to be trucked all the way from Edmonton. People in Medicine Hat have natural gas in their basements, but because of this additional horrendous tax increase, their utility bills are twice the level they were just a year ago.

speechtext: I wonder if they tax Quebec electricity.

speechtext: It is natural gas that is taxed. Electricity is produced in central Canada and, of course, there are too many voters there, so electricity is not taxed.

speechtext: They took off the export tax.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
But it is all right to tax natural gas because there are not many Liberal voters in Medicine Hat anyway.
I read in the newspaper yesterday or today that the beavers in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources are working on the so-called son of the National Energy Program. They are going to produce some documents. They are worried about criticism and the obvious fact that the National Energy Program is a disaster. They are worried about the observations being made by everyone that the National Energy Program is a disaster. Those observations are not being made just by politicians but by literally everyone in the country involved in business in any way, shape or form. They are going to produce a new paper called "The son of the National Energy Program" which apparently will say that the National Energy Program is alive and well and on schedule. The National Energy Program might be alive and well, but the country is dying of it. If we

May 13, 1982
Taxation
want to revive the economy and the country, the best way to do it is to kill the National Energy Program.
The government told us the three goals of the National Energy Program were self-sufficiency, Canadianization and fair revenue sharing. Everyone supports those goals. The problem is that the National Energy Program is working against the achievement of every one of them. It is working against self-sufficiency. Self-sufficiency is out the window. We will not have it in this generation or in this century. We will not come anywhere near self-sufficiency. That is the conclusion of the National Energy Board and everyone else who has looked at the energy situation.
With respect to Canadianization, between 1975 and 1980 the degree of Canadian ownership of the oil and gas industry increased very substantially. That was before the National Energy Program. All that happened in 1975 was that the tax law was changed to put Canadians on a par with foreigners for the first time in history with respect to investment in Canada. That was all. The tax law just put Canadians on a par, and the degree of Canadianization or growth in the Canadian-owned sector of the industry grew spectacularly. The National Energy Program finished that. It drove Canadians out of Canada. There are more Canadian companies with offices in Denver than there were Canadian offices in Calgary ten years ago. Downtown Denver looks like Calgary did four or five years ago. Buildings are being put up by Canadians and filled by Canadian oil companies.
In order to Canadianize the Canadian oil and gas industry, the minister's officials telephoned companies in 1981 and said: "We want to encourage Canadianization; we would like you to look into acquiring some American-owned oil and gas companies." The banks were telephoned and told this was government policy and that the government wanted them to cooperate. Many companies accepted those blandishments. Such companies were Dome, Sulpetro, Turbo, Drummond and Husky. They said, "Hey, this is a good idea. The banks want to give us money, and the government thinks it is a good idea. We are being encouraged and applauded."
Seven and a half billion dollars left the country. Not one new job was created. Not one new barrel of oil was added. There has not been a single benefit to the country in terms of achieving real goals. Foreign-owned companies have become for the most part Canadian owned, but every single one of those companies today has regret because they are all in deep trouble. They are in such deep trouble that the bankers who lent them money are in trouble. The latest estimate is that there might be as much as $5 billion in uncollectable bank loans outstanding in Canada. That is just absolute insanity. Why would the country spend $7.5 billion and not get a single job out of it? We did not get a single extra barrel of oil out of it. We did not get a single extra cubic foot of gas out of it. There has been absolutely no benefit. We have crippled the companies which were enticed by the blandishments of the minister and his officials. What incredible stupidity!
In the meantime, that $7.5 billion was joined by about $10 billion of capital. Investors said: "I guess we are not welcome in this country," and they left. Canadian and foreign money
totalling about $17.5 billion also left. When that happened, the dollar was put under pressure. To keep the dollar from falling through the floor, we have to keep interest rates high. The interest rates we have are much higher than necessary because of the stupid National Energy Program. It is supposed to Canadianize. What has happened is just incredible.
Then there is the claim of fair revenue sharing. From each barrel of oil produced the federal government collects 44 per cent of the revenue. The people who go out to find the oil, the people who take the risk of acquiring the land, the people who take the risk in doing the geophysical work, the people who take the risk in drilling the oil, the people who take the risk putting the system in place, the people who take the risk building the pipelines and who do everything else, get 7 per cent of the revenue while the others get 44 per cent. Is that fair revenue sharing? It has resulted in fewer companies searching for oil; it has caused lay-offs; it has caused companies to go bankrupt; it has caused companies to leave the country; it has caused carnage in what previously was a buoyant and growing industry which generated jobs all across the country. That is what "fair revenue sharing" has done, Mr. Speaker.
Some weeks ago the province of Alberta reacted to the devastation and carnage by adjusting its royalty rates. I do not know of anyone who criticized that move. The federal government needs to show that it is equally concerned by making the same move and I am pleased to note that the minister has not rejected that notion. He has kept the door open. If the gossip columnists in the newspapers are right, he is engaged in a debate with the Department of Finance. Apparently that department wants the money and is not willing to give it up. If that argument really is going on, I would be on the minister's side.
I am absolutely convinced and 1 think it can be demonstrated that if the federal government would back off some of these taxes, the resulting stimulus to the economy would generate more revenue to the government than it would lose. People would be put back to work and would pay taxes rather than receive unemployment insurance benefits. Perhaps some Canadian companies who deserted the country as a result of the National Energy Program in 1981 would be encouraged to return and devote their energies and skills, which we certainly need, to activities in this country.
There does not seem to be much that we can do about this Mr. Speaker. I have been objecting for a long time and mine is not a voice in the wilderness. There is a veritable Mormon Tabernacle Choir out there which has been objecting for a year and a half.
I wonder if it was necessary to go through the pain of this carnage or if we could not have had a different system, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps in the first instance we could have avoided the mistake that is the National Energy Program if we had opened up the policy-making process, as the Minister of Finance is now talking about opening up the budgetary
May 13, 1982

process. Perhaps all of government should be opened up. There should be some scrutiny of the advice given to the minister by his officials on the energy policy process. We should be able to make an analysis of the data that are given to him as facts. I know they were not facts. The information could have been the result of error or it could have been cooked, but it certainly was not factual.
I wonder if things would have been different if the minister had listened to the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada. After the National Energy Program was introduced, it asked him to refer the matter to a standing committee of the House or to a joint committee of the Senate and the House for study. If the minister had agreed and there had been an opportunity for full discussion and analysis of that program 15 months ago, then perhaps we could have foreseen the consequences for Canada. Perhaps we could have avoided some of the worst consequences if the matter had been fully aired. How many billions of dollars or hundreds of thousands of jobs could have been saved? How many companies could have avoided bankruptcy if there had been fair and open and honest debate among parliamentarians?
When the Independent Petroleum Association said that the national energy policy was going to be a disaster for the country, the minister said that the association had no credibility. As a result, the head of Petro-Canada quit the association because it did not have nice things to say about the government. I wonder if things would have been different if the minister had listened, instead of discounting the credibility of the association. Would they have been different if the head of Petro-Canada had listened to the association instead of quitting? If the matter had been referred to a committee for study, I wonder how many people would be working today who are presently unemployed, wondering how they are going to maintain their standard of living and keep a roof over their head.
Is it not time that we demanded that the bureaucrats who actually run the government come out into the light? It is time we had an open democracy so that we can see what they are doing and perhaps prevent the terrible mistakes that are destroying the country.
I had hoped that the minister would announce some changes in the incremental oil revenue tax and the petroleum and gas revenue tax. The small producers have been lobbying the minister for over a year and I had hoped that he would do something for them along the lines of their suggestions. It appears that my hopes were in vain, Mr. Speaker, although there is still time left in the debate and committee stage is still to come. Perhaps the minister can bring himself to admit that his advisers are not doing well by him. I hope that he will admit that it is time to stop devastating the oil and gas industry. It is time we got back to the position we were in before the National Energy Program was introduced. We must be able to pursue self-sufficiency, Canadianization, and growth. We must be able to adopt a positive outlook and direct our efforts to making this country work. We continue to hope for all that, Mr. Speaker, although only a fool would hold his breath waiting for it.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-112 is the new version of the former Bill C-93 which dealt with the energy taxes, namely, the tax on industrial gas only consumed domestically, changes to the petroleum and gas revenue tax or PGRT, and implementation of the oil revenue tax, the IORT.
The hon. member who has just spoken was talking about taxes. No one likes to pay taxes, Mr. Speaker, least of all the oil industry. At the committee hearings which are presently continuing, the president of Dome Petroleum, Mr. Richards, answered a few questions that I put to him about the taxes that the company paid. Dome Petroleum is the largest Canadian-owned oil company in Canada today. It is not Petro-Canada but Dome Petroleum that is the largest. Dome Petroleum was going to receive from the government about S640 million in grants over the next three years. Mr. Richards himself is reputed to be making in the neighbourhood of $600,000 a year, according to the book "The Blue-Eyed Sheiks". Dome Petroleum does not pay taxes. Some oil companies do not like paying taxes; Dome is one.
This is simply an incredible thing to have to explain to your constituents. I represent a working class riding in the east end of Vancouver. My constituents work hard and their income tax is taken right off the top of their cheques, yet here is an outfit like Dome which pays no taxes.
I know the last speaker is a spokesman for the oil industry, and I know people in the industry wonder why the public is not sympathetic to them. Well, when you go around like the hon. member calling everyone stupid, strutting and fretting, ranting and raving, it is sometimes hard to get people to listen to you.
I am going to refer to this later on because I think small oil and gas producers in Canada have some case to take to the government about changes in taxation. However, what I hope to do in my speech today is to tackle this Liberal government and make some criticisms in areas I think are solid. If the members to my right would listen for a change instead of ranting and raving, they might learn something.
I am a western Canadian MP from a consumer area of the country, but I have also spent a lot of time in a producing area. I am going to make some detailed and solid suggestions which the government might consider. I think that is the way to approach things because Canadians are tired of federal-provincial and Liberal-Conservative bickering. They want some suggestions for solutions to the problems. I may be wrong, Mr. Speaker, but I think that is what Canadians want and I propose to make a few today.
I am going to deal with three areas on behalf of the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker. One area is the taxation itself, the PGRT and the IORT, and what they mean. I am also going to deal with the natural gas and gas liquids tax which is levied after the gas reaches the city gate and which represents about 65 per cent of the burner-tip price of $5.51 per mcf.

The government backed off after some strong opposition. But what it did was to bring in a general tax on all gas, and that tax is really hurting consumers. speechtext:
Getting back to the more mundane matter of my speech on taxes, the third area I want to deal with is the agreement with Alberta and what it means to the Canadian consumer. During the period 1973-80 the Canadian public became largely disillusioned with the oil industry for several legitimate reasons. I hope the oil industry will listen to this. I have noted some industry people are writing in Oilweek and other energy magazines who have started to look at the issue as dispassionately as they can. If they do, they can make a solid case where they have one. In my view, the Canadian public saw first of all that the price paid for domestic oil was no longer related to the cost of production, but was being legislated in response to the arbitrary prices set by OPEC. We call them the Arabs, but they are not all Arabs. It was seen that this cartel was really determining prices in Canada.
Second, Mr. Speaker, the price increases were, by and large, not benefiting the Canadian public or the Canadian-owned portion of the oil and gas industry. Instead, the increases were contributing billions of dollars to the assets of the large foreign-owned corporations which had established reserves. For example, for every $1 increase in the price of conventional oil, it is estimated that the value of the reserves of Imperial, Amoco, Texaco, Shell and Gulf rises by more than $4 billion. We have to remember that this is a country which allowed as much as 75 per cent of its oil industry to be dominated by foreign-owned oil companies. It is really shameful that we did that. So every time we increased the price of oil, we gave these people more money. It is a wonderful scheme if you are a large, multinational oil company.
The assets of the industry as a whole increased by 260 per cent between 1973 and 1980. I understand that now industry profits have gone down and they have cash flow problems, but between 1973 and 1980 they made a heck of a lot of money. These gains seem particularly unfair to the Canadian public which had subsidized through taxation and super-depletion allowances the discovery of these reserves. So the consumer is paying once with the subsidies, paying again at the pump, and now they are going to be asked to pay a third time with increased taxes; but I will come to that in a minute.
Another reason the Canadian public was suspicious is that although the industry and governments had assured the public there was no shortage of crude oil and subsequently promoted
large exports to the United States, by 1974 the reserve figures had been altered so dramatically that it was forecast that Canada would be a net importer of crude oil by the end of the decade. Understandably the public was shocked and appalled by this turn of events and demanded that the government start collecting and distributing accurate information on Canada's energy future.
Everyone knows that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) once said in this House that we have enough conventional oil reserves for 300 years. Now it is about nine to 11 years. On the basis of what that minister said, we exported one-half our daily production, and that is why this government has all the problems it has today, because we are self-sufficient in all forms of energy except oil. We are going to do the same thing with our natural gas. We are on the point of exporting that as well, and in a few years we may have the same problem with natural gas.
Our party, Mr. Speaker, sharing these concerns, forced the minority Liberal government to form a public energy corporation which could provide accurate technical information on the oil and gas industry to the government, which in turn would earn profits for the Canadian people from the development of Canadian resources. That company is PetroCan. It belongs to us. For the same reasons there was a limited movement towards this end in Alberta when that province formed the Alberta Energy Company, which was involved in Syncrude. By 1980, Mr. Speaker, the oil and gas industry was by far the most profitable industrial sector of the Canadian economy. In fact, in Alberta it became almost impossible to raise investment capital, I am told, for anything but oil and gas exploration.
This sets the background to why the government would come in with some taxes to tax away these windfall revenues. It was to be expected, but the problem is that it may be killing the goose by the manner in which it levied the taxes.
The Liberal government's answer to the growing problem was the National Energy Program. I agree with the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) in the sense that perhaps there was not a problem, but it was a rich industry and the money was flowing to few individuals and to many multinational oil companies, and this was money from Canadian consumers, so the government was bound to take some of that windfall back in the form of taxes. This was done in the United States. It enacted a windfall profits tax after the OPEC oil increases. It was perfectly in keeping with what had happened in other areas. The American ambassador may be surprised to learn that the United States did exactly the same thing.
While the thrust of the National Energy Program to Canadianize is correct and while its thrust to obtain a larger share of revenues from the industry is correct, the problem is that it is hurting independent Canadian companies by imposing a more complicated tax environment and by emphasizing
May 13, 1982

development of frontier areas which are in the control of the oil giants. These submissions were given to the committee. We sent an economics committee from our caucus across the country. We went to Alberta and listened to the Alberta Energy Services Association, to some oil companies and oil groups, and to some servicing groups. If we could take away the Canadian Petroleum Association and if we could cut through all the guff, we would see that there was a problem for small companies because of the complicated tax environment. Also we would see that the NEP was taking the action out of Alberta and moving it to frontier areas. Of course, that was part of the war between federal and provincial governments. It was hurting small Canadian companies and was helping the oil giants which the National Energy Program was supposed to curb in the first place. This is the real critique of the National Energy Program.
Moreover, the federal government unilaterally increased its share of the the energy resource revenue pie without making any significant commitment to encourage domestic conservation, alternate fuels, or expansion of domestic use of our relatively abundant supplies of natural gas and heavy oil. I know that there are provisions in the National Energy Program for alternatives and conservation, but they are far outweighed by the emphasis upon supply and upon going to the Beaufort Sea and Hibernia to find new oil. I think we must find new oil and we have to develop Hibernia, for example. We need oil in Canada. We cannot be ostrichlike in our critique of the government. But more could have been done in the area of conservation.
Last week I saw an advertisement in the magazine Oilweek in which a company was advertising a heat pump. It claimed that if heat pumps were installed in houses it would save something like 80 per cent of energy used. It was broken down per barrel, but unfortunately I did not bring the article with me. However, I will raise this matter again in committee debate on the bill. If I read the advertisement correctly, it seemed to indicate that we could save two, three or four oil sands plants by simply bringing heat pumps to all homes in Canada. This would provide employment. It is the kind of thing we should be doing instead of megaprojects. But that is another subject; I was discussing the National Energy Program.
Then there was an agreement between the federal government and Alberta which was signed on September 1, 1981. The agreement was premised upon rapidly rising world prices for crude oil throughout the decade. That premise has been shown to be wrong. In all my reading, I see a stable environment or a stable price for OPEC oil in the next decade. This makes sense for OPEC; if one thinks about it, one will realize that it is in the interests of OPEC. I see a stable price, not a rapidly rising one. The problem is that the National Energy Program and the agreement with Alberta were designed on a false premise, namely, simply to stuff more petrodollars into the federal deficit and the heritage fund without regard to either domestic producers or consumers.

I hesitate to mention this, but if there is a lesson one must learn from the Saskatchewan election, perhaps it is that a government with lots of money in its heritage fund and in its provincial coffers does not necessarily mean that the average grassroots person thinks he or she is receiving benefits. That was the problem in the agreement with Alberta. There was lots of money brought into the coffers of the federal government and into the Alberta heritage fund, but it does not help the man and woman in Vancouver-Kingsway, the man and woman in Spadina, or the farmers in the various ridings which my colleagues represent.
After ten years of acrimonious debate between the federal government and the government of Alberta, we have the worst of all possible worlds. We have high consumer prices and therefore increased tension between the producing and consuming provinces. We have a domestic industry which is in serious trouble. We have a deteriorating domestic supply of crude oil.
For the benefit of my friends on my right who are fond of heckling me, let me repeat that we have the worst of all possible worlds with the Liberal energy policy. We have high consumer prices when we were promised low prices; we have a domestic industry which is in serious trouble when we were promised a program to help small Canadian producers; and we have a deteriorating domestic supply of crude oil when we were promised energy self-sufficiency. Is that not the situation today?
Are there any solutions to these problems? Let me suggest some solutions, some of which are new ideas. It seems to me that one problem faced by small companies in western Canada is shut-in natural gas. They have trouble selling natural gas. The government should look at the possibility of a public natural gas bank, consisting of gas received instead of some provincial royalties. Of course, there would have to be an agreement with the producing provinces. If Alberta did this, in lieu of 20 per cent in natural gas royalties, it would increase the market for natural gas by some 10 per cent.
We could aid the provinces in the construction of facilities for the production of high quality gasoline from natural gas feed stocks, following the process developed by Mobil and currently underway in Germany and New Zealand. This facility would create an additional local market in Alberta alone of 5 per cent.
We could bring in a program to encourage maximum substitution of natural gas for heating oil and gasoline. I know there is a program in place, but we have done very little with our automobile and truck fleets. Most hon. members with offices in the Confederation Building come to the House on a bus. That bus is one of a fleet of buses. By what is it propelled? Is it propelled by natural gas? No, it is propelled by scarce gasoline. We could do much more here.
Another area in which we could become involved is the expansion of heavy oil in the west. The federal government, should immediately construct, in co-operation with the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, one or more heavy-oil upgraders which would provide necessary facilities to expand

May 13, 1982

the Lloydminster, Wainwright and Cold Lake heavy oil fields. Such development should emphasize small-scale modules, and in situ miniprojects which would provide a much needed shot in the arm to both the drilling and service industry and smaller, independent, Canadian-controlled companies.
As much as we talk about Alsands, that kind of project would not have helped small drillers in Alberta. There is no doubt that the spin-offs will help some of the industry. If you really want to help the small, independent companies they would be better served in the areas of heavy oil and small drilling projects, not in mining, which is what Alsands was. This provides an economic alternative to the uneconomic Alsands megaproject route.
Second, the federal government could improve prices for heavy oil to bring on stream otherwise semi-marginal deposits.
Third, we could have a public heavy-oil bank, assisted in the process by a deferred royalty on heavy-oil payments. This would allow a shorter pay-out period while protecting the royalty share in Alberta, for example. There could be public participation with Petro-Canada, the Alberta Energy Company or Saskoil, or other miniprojects at manageable levels and economic prices.
What we could do for the Canadian industry is to replace the unfair and overly complex tax regime, the PGRT and the IORT that we are debating in this bill, with a simple federal and provincial royalty sharing agreement, analogous to the tax rental agreement.
I would like to expand on that particular matter. It may be the crux of the problem with this bill. Rather than face the problem of revenue sharing in a straightforward and rational way, the federal and provincial governments have engaged in a series of tax wars which have continued to the present time. They have burdened the oil and gas industry with one of the most complicated and consequently unfair tax regimes in Canada. This regime must be changed. Overly complex taxes are unfair taxes. To the largest corporations, these taxes become fine instruments to be tuned and played by well-paid accounting staffs for the benefit of corporate interests. On the other hand, for the small, independent Canadian producer, they represent a mountain of paperwork and added expense.
What we need is further price negotiations between Ottawa and Edmonton. The provincial government should consider voluntarily sharing a portion of its provincial royalties with the federal government. This would eliminate any justification for the PGRT, the IORT and excise taxes and would hopefully give the provincial government more say in what the surrendered revenues would be used for.
This is a novel suggestion. Some people may say it is naive or wishful thinking, but I believe there is a political will within the country for the producing provinces like Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia to arrive at better agreements with the federal government. The oil agreement that the Premier of Alberta and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) toasted on September 1, 1981, is gone. It has become redundant because the price of oil on the world market is not going
up. The tax regime so instituted is too complicated for Canadian industry, especially small industry. If it is redundant, let us change it.
There is another approach I would like to put forward on behalf of our party. We do not support the concept of giving tax incentives or bonuses without earning an interest in the particular venture. Therefore, if there are to be grants by either the federal or provincial government of up to 80 per cent of the cost of a well, we say that either the provincial or the federal government should get that share of equity in the well. We believe that there have been vast giveaways in that area.
The introduction of equity incentives, federal-provincial royalty sharing and the elimination of complex federal taxes would require a careful review of the existing royalty structures. This has to be done at the provincial level and done with federal-provincial co-operation. The object would be to simplify the taxation regime of the industry and not to fatten the coffers of the provincial governments.
I think I have made some positive suggestions about how to deal with an industry which appears to be ailing. I do not think I have strutted or fretted or called everyone stupid. I believe that my criticisms of this government have been just as effective as the criticisms of my friends to my right. They have made some changes and they will have to continue to do so.
I mentioned the tax on domestically consumed natural gas. That affects every member opposite because I suspect that most of them have people in their ridings who use natural gas. The tax on that natural gas is unfair and regressive. It affects senior citizens, people on fixed incomes and poor people just as much as, or perhaps more so than, the rich person because they spend a greater proportion of their income on such things as energy, food and housing. I believe that this tax is a regressive one and should be removed.
Total energy costs, as measured by a component of the consumer price index, have gone up 46 per cent since 1980 under the Liberals. Natural gas prices rose 28 per cent in 1981. The present cost to consumers for oil and gas will double by 1986. I am already receiving complaints from constituents in my riding who tell me that while their salary went up 8 per cent or 9 per cent, their energy costs are going up 28 per cent. They ask me what is going on. It cannot be explained. It is a regressive tax which should be removed.
I have already spoken about the PGRT. It is a very complicated matter. This royalty has certain advantages because it is put on at the wellhead, which makes it difficult to manipulate in order to deduct expenses at that stage. As I said, though, the problem is that it will hurt the small producers. I have suggested some ways to replace that tax with a method of sharing provincial royalties with the federal government, which may work.
During the committee hearing I would like to raise the matter of oil companies which have received a windfall gain from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) for one quarter in 1981 in which no higher taxes were levied. What
May 13, 1982

happened at that time was that the government boosted the price of oil by $2.50 a gallon for three months, from October 1 to December 31, 1981. However, the taxes did not come in until January 1. Therefore, the government may talk tough with the oil companies but they gave them a windfall profit for those three months. I want to press the government on that matter during the committee hearing and perhaps introduce an amendment to the bill which would provide that this money be paid back to the Canadian consumer.
I would like to conclude by saying that the Canadian consumer is getting hosed by a Liberal government that promised during the election campaign that it would bring in lower energy costs. The official opposition have been roaming around the country, including Saskatchewan, saying that they are a party of low energy prices. Do not believe it. In the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) when he was Minister of Finance, there as an initial 18-cent per gallon levy and it was going to rise further. People forget that fact. Let us not make any mistake about it: the Conservatives are the high energy cost party and they are being followed by the Liberal Party. I suggest to hon. members to my right that they review the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West and cut out the malarkey in the House of Commons.

I have listened to this argument going on for a long time in this House, and I find that there have been two very interesting arguments, especially of late. One of them is that a terrible

tragedy has been brought on by this government's National Energy Program and its policies because we are not taking that oil and gas out of the ground fast enough. The argument is that we have to get it out of the ground, we have to continue to explore and we have to sell that oil. There is a kind of inference there that there must be a hole or something beneath the earth's crust and that all the oil will disappear into the hole, that it will run away if we do not get it out fast!
No one in this House has told me that in the long run we are not going to run out of conventional crude oil. We talk about cutting back to about 10 per cent of supplies in the 1980s by the early 1990s. Because of new discoveries, certainly the Hibernia, the north and other factors I will come to in a minute, we will probably not be down to that point so early. We may get a couple of years' grace.
We keep hearing that if we do not explore, drill and pump the oil and gas out immediately, it will not be there. Somehow it will disappear and be lost to us. We hear that it is a terrible crime not to take out the oil at this point. Future generations will want that opportunity in the next 10 or 20 years, but we do not hear about that. The exploration does not have to be done tomorrow, next year or ten years down the line. The oil is not going to disappear. There are no perforations in the caps on the national gas wells which will allow the gas to leak away.
There are over a thousand wells that have been drilled and capped. We are told it is a terrible thing that the gas was not taken out right away. 1 have great difficulty understanding that kind of mentality. We were told by the minister of energy, mines and resources in the Clark government that the crossover time between the supply and demand for natural gas and western reserves would be 1997. It may have been extended a bit, but it is still there. It will still be a resource that our children and our children's children will have a hard time finding.
The fact that we are not selling or exporting this gas immediately is not a tragedy for Canadians, it is a good thing. It is and will remain a valuable resource even though it is not being pumped out now. That is a myth that must be dispelled immediately.
There is another myth we constantly hear from the Tory opposition. If a company buys a property or the controlling interest in another company, that is considered an investment. That investment is made in the expectation that there will be some profit. That is the way business works. It is a legitimate function.
However, if the government should buy Petrofina, Phillips Petroleum or Atlantic Richfield, that is an expenditure and the money is wasted. They say that money is being thrown away by purchasing such a company. That is what we hear. They believe that if the government buys it, it is not an investment, not profitable and will not yield a return. I have difficulty with this kind of mythology that says that Canadians have no business investing Canadian dollars through the Government
Taxation
of Canada and owning a national oil company. It is something I do not understand.
These two mythologies leave me cold. I am prompted to speak time and time again because they keep coming up. Those opposite always say that we are losing tremendous opportunities by not pumping the oil and gas out of the ground. They say we should be exporting it. They also say the government has no business buying a company because that is an expenditure and a waste of government funds.
The Tories talk about when they were in government. One reason they are no longer in power is that they do not understand the Canadian public. Canadians respected the notion of this government forming Petro-Canada. They liked that idea. Canadians, through their government, want to own a strong, powerful, active company, one involved in exploration and the sale of gas at the pumps.
When I drive around this city or Thunder Bay, I am pleased to see the Canadian flags and the name Petro-Canada. I feel good about that. We in Thunder Bay were very happy to see the Petro-Canada sign go up. At that point we were the most easterly region where Petro-Canada stations existed. In eastern Canada we now see the sign at stations that were formerly Petrofina.
This is the way Canadians want it to be. It gives them a sense of owning something, of owning part of their own resources. I am proud to be part of the government which brought that about. I know I will hear the argument from the New Democratic Party that they were responsible for Petro-Canada. However, I was at the caucus meeting where this idea was presented. We were a part of selling that idea. The minister talked about it long before it became an issue, long before the so-called "forced" vote. It was eight or ten months before that happened.
Six or eight months before the debate in this House, I attended a convention of our party where this idea was strongly suggested. There is no question that the NDP were very interested and wanted the same thing, but to say they brought it about is not true. The truth is that it came out of this government. There was a lot of work done by many of us in this party, and I resent being told that somebody else do it. When we were in power in 1974, we were not under the gun. It was not a minority situation at that time. That is when this proposal was brought in. Nobody forced us to do it.
It is interesting to note that the Petro-Canada bill was one of five bills brought in at that time. The NDP energy critic, Tommy Douglas, a long-term member of this House and a great Canadian, attended the committee meetings on that bill and supported this government in every respect. He supported second reading in principle, supported the bill in committee, introduced amendments that were accepted and supported the bill all the way through. Other members of his party did the same. He did the same with regard to the emergency supplies allocation bill, the monitoring bill, the Petroleum Administration Act, in fact, all five bills. They were supported by the NDP and filibustered by the Tories.

May 13, 1982
Taxation
Now here we have the granddaddy of them all, the bill that says to the people of this country, in fact throughout the world, that we are determined to get control of a resource that should be Canadian. We are determined that we are going to be owners of our own natural resources. This is the bill that says we are going to do it. This is the bill that the people on the left are with. It is the one bill that Mr. Douglas came to speak to our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about, and I am very pleased that he did, to give him support, he and a bunch of other Canadians, good Canadians from all over the country. They came down to see our Prime Minister and said they support what we are doing in this bill. But not that other party. I am very disappointed that when we get to the crux of the debate-the bill that Mr. Douglas said he would like to have had ten years ago-that support is not there.
That is why I am proud to be on this side of the House as a Liberal, speaking about our energy policy. I admit that it is not easy right now, that these are difficult times for the National Energy Program and that things may look tough in these difficult times; but in the long run there will be hundreds of billions of dollars for Canadians when we hold and develop our own resources.
In the last few weeks I keep hearing people on the other side and even some on this side being called socialists. There is that kind of talk. The word "socialism" is some kind of word that condemns you, saying you are stupid and do not know what is going on, that you are destructive. It is a word I find used with much disdain by many people on the other side. Certainly on this side of the House there is no one who is a pure socialist, a socialist per se. We as Canadians are a people who believe in a mixed economy. I do not know that there are many people on the other side who would say that we should sell Ontario Hydro back to a private corporation. I do not know how many would sell OC Transpo or the Toronto transportation system or the Thunder Bay transportation system back to the private sector. It makes sense to run them as public enterprises. I suppose you could call that socialism. If Ontario Hydro is called socialism, it was probably put into effect by a Conservative government. You could call the CBC, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, socialist. Pacific Western Airlines was purchased as a private company by the government of Alberta and made into a socialist enterprise, but I do not call Mr. Lougheed a socialist. I do not call the Premier of Ontario at the time who bought Ontario Hydro and made it into a public corporation a socialist. Because I am proud to be part of the formation of Petro-Canada, I do not call myself a socialist.
I believe there is a decent, intelligent mix between the private and public sectors in a democratic country like ours. Some may say we should lean a little more this way, others may say we should lean a little more the other way; but basically speaking, that mix is a decent mix.
I do not believe that the kind of mix that President Reagan would have in the United States is the kind I would like. I think there are more valuable things being done in the public sector than he believes in. For instance, I believe strongly that our medical and health care system in Canada is better than
any in the world. I would not want that to be turned back to some kind of private insurance company to operate. I do not know how many on the other side would want that to happen. But because I say it, I am called a socialist. The word does not mean anything. It is a word that deals with the extent to which people organize their affairs either in the private sector or in the public sector, and that mix is always there. To say this group is socialist and that the others are free enterprisers is just using two blurred terms.
With Canadian ownership of, first, the oil and gas industry, these particular enterprises, we are not saying the Canadian government is going to buy up all of the multinational controlled companies. We are going to buy up some of them and we are making it possible for other parts of the industry to fall into the hands of Canadian companies.
When Nova Corporation-it was not Nova Corporation at the time, it was Alberta Gas-purchased Husky, almost simultaneously we bought Phillips Petroleum. I thought this was a great combination. I was quite pleased in many ways that Petro-Canada did not get Husky. At the time I felt rather badly about it, but I thought better about it afterwards. What happened was that we did not spend our money on Husky but we got Phillips, and Alberta Gas, or the Nova Corporation, bought Husky. In those particular deals we ended up with two good American companies that had become part of Canada. Was that not a sound proposition? It seems to me it was not a socialist proposition. It was a proposition where we as Canadians worked out a mix between the private sector and the public sector which was a very valuable and very good mix.
So, Mr. Speaker, I welcome this particular program because it enables us to put control back into the hands of Canadians, whether it be through the public sector or through the private sector, and more can be done through the private sector than through the public sector. We get it back into our hands so that we can control those resources. We will be able to control the kind of development we want from those resources. We can decide whether we want to develop those resources instantly or leave them there, knowing full well that there is no hole in the ground that they are going to disappear into or that the caps are not perforated, that they will be there for a long time.
Even though it is a difficult time, Mr. Speaker, and even though it is not easy sitting on this side to be buffeted constantly, I really feel proud to be able to say that we believe in something and we stand up for it. I believe in the National Energy Program. In the long run, in the history of Canada it will prove to be a very important development and I am proud to have been here in the last ten years to be part of that development.
