speechtext:
That an humble Address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all minutes of meetings, letters and other communications during the last year between the government and the representatives of airline companies in connection with the division of landing rights and other services between Dorval and Mirabel airports in Quebec.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion is certainly appropriate at this time when we anticipate that within the next week or two we shall hear some announcement from the government about its intentions with regard to these two airports, Dorval and Mirabel.
To put the subject in the proper context, I would like to go back over the history of the past three decades. When I came here from Scotland after the war, I came over on a Northstar into Dorval airport. I remember well that I was so happy to get off that aircraft that it would not have mattered what kind of airport I was landing at. In fact, I disliked the flight on that Northstar from Scotland to Dorval so much that I would not travel in an aircraft for the next 15 years.
Be that as it may, it was interesting to watch the development of Dorval. In those days it was obviously not intended for use as a major international North American airport. Dorval was the first airport to undergo extensive renovations, alterations and additions, and in those days the work that was being done in Dorval was a great assist to my own industry, the construction industry. Plans were developed and the building got underway.
I recall that at that time many criticisms were made of the design of Dorval and that, when the airport at Toronto was to
Airport Services
be built-or rebuilt-that particular design would certainly not be used. The concept at Dorval at that time was an open one, and even today the availability of space is such that there is really no difficulty whatsoever in providing the accommodation needed for automobiles and other forms of traffic going into and out of Dorval. Access is easy and fast.
When the Toronto airport was built in its present form, it was decided that it would be a more modern airport, so it was built, as everyone knows, in an entirely different form and concept. I know this too well because I had what I suppose I could call the misfortune of having to go through that airport once a week, as I had an office in Toronto, and many was the time I was stuck in a taxi approaching the airport and watching my plane take off because I could not get into that airport.
Being proud of Montreal and always somewhat jealous of Toronto construction, I obviously felt we had made the right decision at that time. However, the years went by and it again became obvious that additional work had to be done at Dorval. In the mid-sixties when I was president of the Montreal Construction Association we were making representations to senior cabinet ministers at that time, and plans had been made both to extend and to widen the runways. The intention was to turn Dorval into an airport which would be good for the next 20 or 30 years. Rather strangely, the local mayors resisted any further expansion at Dorval. What had happened was that there had been considerable house building in the vicinity of the airport. People had even built houses in line with the runways, and suddenly they were objecting to the fact that planes were going overhead, despite the fact that the airport was there first and they built their houses later. They objected to the airplanes and made representations through their elected representatives at the municipal level that the amount of traffic at Dorval should be cut down, to the point that night traffic at Dorval was not allowed, and it is still not allowed.
This obviously took away the effectiveness of Dorval as an international airport, to the point where the government had little choice but to decide to build a second airport, leaving at that time Dorval to service the continental traffic, with Mirabel obviously to become the international centre. I say Mirabel because prior to deciding on that region a study was undertaken, and the area which was chosen for this new international airport was my own constituency of Vaudreuil. That was vigorously opposed by the Quebec provincial government because of its proximity to the Ontario border. The provincial government refused to give its approval of the site on the basis that some of the benefits from this development in the constituency of Vaudreuil would accrue to the province of Ontario. The choice of the provincial government, as we well know, was the south shore. The eventual compromise site was Ste. Scholastique, which is now Mirabel, and construction got underway. Surrounding land was expropriated. It is rather interesting now that there are complaints from the people whose land was expropriated that an attempt was made at that time by the government to expropriate land to make sure

May 13, 1982
Airport Services
Mirabel would never be in the position in which Dorval found itself when it was not able to expand its runways as it would have liked.
The airport at Mirabel was eventually opened, at a cost of some $1 billion, in 1975 and, according to the projections made prior to the decision to build the airport, there was to be an annual increase in passenger traffic which warranted the construction of that second airport.
However, there were two subsequent events which changed that projected increase in passenger traffic. The very first one was the decision of the government to allow foreign airlines to enter Canada at Toronto rather than Montreal. Of course, the foreign airlines immediately took advantage of that permission and, as a result, the Montreal area was no longer the point of entry for many of those foreign airlines. The second event was the economic downturn which resulted in less use of airlines.
The decision to construct Mirabel, the second airport in the Montreal area and a truly international airport from the point of view of its size, its quality and its capability of handling all kinds of aircraft, including the largest aircraft presently flying, cargo planes and so forth, was a wise one based on the conditions which existed at that time.
And, as everyone knows, subsequently the same logic was applied to the construction of a second airport at Toronto. However, the people of Toronto resisted the construction of the Pickering airport and, as a result, a move was made to expand the existing Toronto airport. For those of us who use the Toronto airport it possibly was a reasonable compromise, but of one thing 1 am absolutely convinced: ten years from now we in Montreal will be very pleased that we have two airports.
To return to the immediate problem, the Dorval airport cannot handle 24 hour per day traffic. Second, because of the length and width of its runways Dorval would be in a very difficult position if it had to handle all the additional traffic from Mirabel.
I put this on the record because I am going to argue that we should still mothball Mirabel. The problem with transferring any traffic to Mirabel is that some of the passengers who presently fly out of Dorval would not go via Mirabel but instead would go by shuttle service to Toronto, thus increasing the traffic in Toronto and defeating the purpose of the move. At the present time Air Canada runs some of its Caribbean flights via Toronto; the reason for this is that it wants to avoid using Mirabel. The Montreal chamber of commerce believes that any change to Mirabel would result in many airlines leaving Montreal altogether.
We have what is, in my opinion, an even more serious problem, however. At the present time the Dorval airport is the hub of the West Island/Montreal activity. The maintenance facilities are there and one must admit that the language of a large number of the workers at Dorval airport at the present time is English. If any attempt is made to move services to Mirabel, it is unlikely that the present employees at Dorval will be willing to move. They will do what many Anglophones have already done-move out of the province. The result will
be a further decrease in the proportion of Anglophones in Quebec and the reason for that will be the decision of the federal government.
I note from the statistics that whereas the traffic growth in Montreal has been just over 4 per cent per annum, the traffic growth in Toronto has been almost double that. Any attempt to move flights out of Dorval into Mirabel will inevitably increase the amount of traffic in Toronto for the reasons that I have stated.
The airlines themselves have come up with a simple solution-mothball Mirabel. It is understood that the loss at Mirabel is in the order of $1 million per week. The profits at Dorval are probably about $1 million per month. The cost of moving from Dorval to Mirabel is estimated to be in the order of half a billion dollars. This is without taking into consideration the disruption of employees who may or may not decide to make the move when the transfer is made. I do not think the transfer is going to be made for the simple reason that the federal government has a commitment to the West Island community.
In any other province it is possible that persons might be willing to move a distance of 30 or 40 miles from one location to another, but the very sensitive language problem in the province of Quebec means that it is not quite that simple. The probability is that the employees at Dorval will be unwilling to make that move.
It is realized that if Mirabel were mothballed it might be impossible to get all the flights into Dorval. That may be so, but I suggest the consequences would be far less severe than if an attempt were made to take flights out of Dorval and put them into Mirabel.
If one looks at the price tag for the move and compares it with the present $50 million per year loss, it will be seen that if the shift is to cost half a billion dollars and the interest on that amount alone is almost twice the total annual loss, economically it would not make any sense either.
When an international airport is constructed it is essential that there be easy access. Because the government of the province of Quebec was annoyed that it did not get its own way and because the present provincial government has no intention of co-operating with the federal government, there has been a refusal to construct a main highway linking Montreal to Mirabel despite the fact the federal government has offered the financing. It makes absolutely no sense, when the provincial government refuses to construct a high-speed highway linking Montreal to Mirabel, to give any consideration to transferring flights from Dorval to Mirabel which businessmen would refuse to take because of the additional time factor and the additional inconvenience involved. We cannot force people to use a different location if they are not so inclined. Unless all flights were taken out of Dorval, businessmen would still use that airport and travel by the alternative routes I have suggested, such as going via Toronto.
For these reasons, I suggest that any move by the federal government to make any transfer whatsoever of flights from
May 13, 1982

Dorval to Mirabel at the present time would be uneconomical, contrary to the interests of the residents of the West Island of Montreal, would be a very damaging blow to the anglophone community that remains in the province of Quebec, and would be foolhardy in the extreme.
Whether in its wisdom the federal government decides to retain Mirabel for its present international and cargo flights, it must swallow its pride, accept the fact that the decision to construct originally was correct-and as I have said, I fully support the original decision-absorb the inevitable losses and be patient for another five, six or seven years when the people in Montreal and the province of Quebec will be very proud that they have access to two airports in Montreal, Dorval and Mirabel.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) that he will have the full support of hon. members in this party for his Notice of Motion for Production of Papers. I think the hon. member showed considerable courage in making the statement he did about Mirabel today. It is regrettable that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is not here to listen to that statement.
On two successive days, yesterday and today, members of the Liberal caucus from Montreal have raised the concerns of their constituents about the fact that the government is considering actions which would be to their detriment by considering the possibility of transferring a large number of domestic flights from Dorval to Mirabel. That is not in the best interest of the west end of Montreal. The decision clearly would not be in the best interests of the airline industry, which does not want it. Travellers do not want it either and it would be a very regressive step.
From the time the decision was first made to build Mirabel it should have been apparent to the government that it would be a white elephant, extremely costly, underutilized and would cause very serious problems for the future. We have seen those problems manifested in the massive deficit run up by Mirabel, in the treatment of landowners on the site whose farms and homes were taken away from them and who found that their treatment by the government was totally unfair.
We have seen Dorval's competitors advertising for some time to encourage people to route themselves through competing airports. One example is that of a few years ago when people were encouraged to route themselves through Logan instead of Mirabel because it is more convenient. We have seen that the reaction of the travelling public is that they find Mirabel extremely inconvenient and very costly to get to.
Anyone who has gone through Mirabel, Mr. Speaker, recognizes that it is very severely underutilized at the present time. The government's investment there was a mistake in the first place, and it is continuing to cost Canadian taxpayers over the course of time. It would be useful for members to have the opportunity of trying to find public transportation from
Airport Services
downtown Montreal to Mirabel, or to take a cab and pay for the expense of travelling to such a remote location. If they do, they will discover something about the inconvenience that airport has caused for so many of the travelling public. For the government now to be talking about depriving air travellers of services they now have in Dorval and requiring them to use Mirabel is, I feel, a very serious and regressive step.
The real question, Mr. Speaker, is to what extent members of the Quebec Liberal caucus are prepared to speak out against this policy currently under consideration. To what extent are they prepared to put their constituents' interests first and give consideration to the concerns of the travelling public, the airlines, and the people of Montreal. Surely it is time that other members of the Liberal caucus showed the courage shown yesterday by the hon. member for Chateauguay (Mr. Watson) and today by the hon. member for Vaudreuil, and speak out to make it known that the decision under consideration is very regressive.
One need look no further than page 4 of today's Globe and Mail to see that concern is running very deep in that part of Montreal. It quotes the hon. member for Chateauguay as follows:
He said in an interview later that the issue is shaping up into "the biggest political problem in the Montreal area. We'll lose two seats for sure" in that area in the next election if the government's plan goes ahead.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Nonsense.

The hon. member opposite says "nonsense". He is saying nonsense to his own colleague. It was the hon. member for Chateauguay who is quoted in today's Globe and Mail as saying that. Perhaps the hon. member wants to get up and attack his friend, the hon. member for Chateauguay. Perhaps he wants to say that the comments of the hon. member for Vaudreuil, who spoke a few minutes ago, were nonsense. We on this side do not believe they are nonsense. We believe there is a very deep-seated concern among the people of Montreal about this waste and inconvenience. We believe for the government to simply bull ahead and ignore this problem is to do a disservice to all Canadians, in particular the people of Montreal.
We should put on record, Mr. Speaker, that members of the Progressive Conservative Party are prepared to fight for the people of Dorval and west end Montreal. If voices on the other side are silenced, if members of the Quebec Liberal caucus are not prepared to stand up for those people, then members on this side will.
We believe Mirabel was a very serious mistake and it is being compounded today by the consideration of shifting domestic traffic from Dorval to Mirabel which would be very unfair to everyone concerned. The taxpayers of Canada have been forced to subsidize a very costly and unnecessary airport at Mirabel. In that regard 1 disagree with my friend, the hon. member for Vaudreuil. It was a mistake in the first place to have built Mirabel, an airport which served only to take prime farm land out of production and deprive farmers of the opportunity of growing and supplying food to the people of that

May 13, 1982
Airport Services
area. It was a mistake, Mr. Speaker, but let us not compound the mistake today by allowing the Minister of Transport to go ahead and transfer domestic routes from Dorval to Mirabel.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I would underline that the hon. member for Vaudreuil has the full support of members on this side of the House for his motion for the production of papers. If it comes to a vote we are prepared to support him. If it does not come to a vote, it will not be because members on this side have talked it out, thereby preventing members of the House of Commons from expressing themselves in a free vote on this issue. It will be because members on the government side have decided to talk it out and deprive the hon. member for Vaudreuil of the opportunity of having a vote on this motion. The people of Dorval have our support and the hon. member has our support. I hope all members of the House will recognize their responsibility and allow this motion to come to a vote today. I hope members on all sides will support this very reasonable motion.

Mr. Speaker, I will be brief because I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken. We will not contribute to this motion being talked out because we support it. I merely want to say that it is hard to hide an elephant. In fact, you can ask any undertaker-it is even harder to bury one, whether it is white or any other colour.
However, the Liberal government deserves an "E" for effort on Mirabel, because after that fiasco they shuffled much of the expropriated land and much of the costs over to the Department of Public Works accounts from the Ministry of Transport accounts. They wiped out the interest payments on Mirabel and tried to shut the closet door on that. Now the government wants to force passengers and airlines to abandon Dorval in order to try and justify the existence of Mirabel.
The simple fact is that Mirabel covers only 14 per cent of its costs. If one uses the same formula for grain that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is relying on arrived at by one Mr. Snavely, farmers should get $12.90 a bushel for grain. If the minister used the Snavely formula on Mirabel, we would recover 14 per cent of the cost.
The government proposes to transfer long-haul domestic flights from Dorval to Mirabel. That is an expensive proposition at a time when the government says there is no money for other things. First of all it will cost about $400 million to build new hangars, terminals and other facilities at Mirabel, duplicating what we now have at Dorval. As Dorval starts to lose traffic it will start to lose money, and we are back into a different rut.
Mirabel is a one-hour and $40 taxi ride from Montreal, so it is no wonder people do not want to use it. If Mirabel were set up in the same way as Gatwick in England, or Frankfurt in Germany, that might make some sense. Gatwick has a highspeed electric train for the transportation of passengers some 40 miles to London at a cost of $6 or $7, and that might make some sense at Mirabel. Of course passengers are reluctant to use Mirabel and you can hardly blame them. CP Air has
threatened to discontinue non-stop flights from Mirabel to western Canada. Air Canada and CP Air passengers will of course avoid Mirabel. As the hon. member who sponsored this motion has said, they will go via Toronto instead, which not only avoids Mirabel but hurts Dorval as well. Malton airport will be under pressure to handle more traffic as airlines and passengers avoid Mirabel. The department will then use this new problem to justify a new airport at Pickering for which it has already thrown $187 million down the drain.
The need for mega-airports such as Mirabel and Pickering died with the death of the supersonic transport. This is what they were designed for. The visions of the mid and late-1960s was that an airport like Mirabel would be the greatest supersonic transportation airport in the whole world. It was to be the first one as well as the greatest one. This has gone down the drain. I agree with the hon. member that it needs mothballing.
Airport congestion at Malton and Dorval can be solved by improving ground transportation on routes up to 500 to 600 miles. I am referring to bus and rail. This will take some money but not as much as the $ 1 billion which the government has already thrown into Mirabel or the $1.5 billion the government will throw into these projects if it gets away with its plan to shift traffic from Dorval to Mirabel.
In supporting this motion, let me indicate that I have a final solution for Mirabel. The government of the United States purchased some property in Ottawa in order to build a new embassy; the Government of Canada will build a new embassy in Washington. I suggest that if we saw the Mirabel terminal building in half, we could give half of it to the U.S. government for its embassy. It could pay for the bill to move that half to Ottawa. We could transport the other half down to Washington. I suspect that the architect's fees for the new embassy in Washington would cover much of the cost of moving the other half of that terminal building to Washington. Then we would have two embassies. We are good, co-operative international neighbours, and we would not have to put mothballs in the buildings. We could saw the terminal in half, have two embassies, and let farmers return to growing food on the land which the runways occupy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this private members' debate provided by Standing Order 48(2), and specifically to debate Motion No. 96 in the name of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), a motion for the production of all communications between the government and the representatives of airline companies in connection with the division of landing rights and other services between Dorval and Mirabel airports in Quebec.
As we are well aware, the issue of the assignment of traffic between Mirabel and Dorval airports has been with us for a long time. Virtually from the opening of Mirabel, it has been reviewed by successive ministers of transport. The issue is an
May 13, 1982

extremely complex one which has many different technical and economic aspects and is one which affects people from many different sectors of society. For example, it affects business travellers and leisure travellers; people living in the vicinity of Mirabel and people living in the vicinity of Dorval; travellers from other parts of Canada, from the United States, from Europe and from all corners of the world; employees at Mirabel and employees at Dorval.
Clearly each of these sectors will see the issue from their own perspective, as did the three hon. members who have participated thus far in the debate. In addition, the view of different people in these sectors will vary to some considerable extent as a result of personal experience and personal involvement. The situation has been exacerbated by further complexities such as Montreal origin-destination passenger traffic which has not grown as anticipated mainly because of the economic downturn, as mentioned by the hon. member for Vaudreuil. It is not only a Canadian economic downturn but a worldwide one. Another complexity is the increased cost of aviation fuel, which no one mentioned, and the resulting raising of fares. Since Mirabel basically serves international traffic, excluding the United States, passenger traffic growth has been reduced even further by the introduction of more direct flights by domestic and foreign European carriers, to other Canadian cities, thereby reducing the number of connecting passengers at Montreal. This development has taken place despite the moratorium on new foreign carriers at Toronto International Airport since 1976 and considerable efforts in bilateral negotiations to encourage the use of Mirabel.
The present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is vigorously attempting to resolve the Montreal airports issue, and fully intends to be the minister who obtains a government decision on the issue. He is a minister who is not afraid to make tough, unpopular decisions. He is one who makes decisions, keeping in mind what is best for the country in the long term.
I know he will appreciate the debate which is taking place this afternoon because it will certainly help him to come up with a solution that will benefit Canada in the long term. As all hon. members are well aware, on February 12, 1981, the same minister released a report entitled, "An Interim Report On Airport Role Options". This report was the culmination of the first phase of a study which had been undertaken by the Department of Transport, assessing a range of possible traffic assignments for the Montreal airports system. With the release of this interim report, all interested parties were invited to submit comments and concerns on the analysis done to date, with a view to providing a broader input base for the analysis in the second phase of the study.
In total, some 92 interested parties submitted their viewpoints and concerns, with the greatest response being from municipal governments and local chambers of commerce. As well, ten air carrier companies submitted detailed information on the potential cost-revenue implications of transferring additional traffic to Mirabel.
Airport Services
Let me reflect for a moment upon the findings of the first phase of the analysis which are documented in the interim report. The analysis indicated the following:
That the original long-range plan to consolidate most of the commercial air traffic at Mirabel is still the best solution.
I emphasize the words "long-range plan". It continued:
That the timing of any such transfer must be carefully assessed taking into account the anticipated demand; the residual economic life of existing facilities at Dorval; the current availability of under-utilized new facilities at Mirabel; and the impact of substantial traffic reassignment on the social and economic wellbeing of the communities adjacent to the two airports.
It went on to indicate:
-that the focus of the second phase of the study must be on not only the costs and benefits of transferring traffic to Mirabel but also on the optimum timing for any such transfer.
1 also emphasize the word "timing". Many of the submissions made in response to the minister's request for comments attempted to identify the costs which would be incurred by the respective party or interest group as a result of any transfer of traffic to Mirabel.
Needless to say, rarely does the summation of the individual aspects of any transportation issue portray the total effect upon the system. The detailed cost benefit analysis which was undertaken in the second phase of the Montreal study, while taking into consideration the information and concerns contained in the individual submissions, at the same time addressed the question of the total impact on the Montreal airports system. This detailed cost benefit analysis is now being finalized. Regardless of what conclusions the analysis indicates, it is inevitable that the proposed solution, whatever it is, will not fully satisfy all parties. It will not satisfy the parties which I mentioned earlier. I could add others. Whatever solution the minister comes up with, it will not satisfy the mayor of Dorval and the mayor at Mirabel Members of Parliament whose ridings are around Mirabel and Members of Parliament whose ridings are around Dorval, MLAs whose constituencies are around Mirabel and MLAs whose constituencies are around Dorval. His solutions will not satisfy local businesses, because whatever move the minister makes, some businesses will be affected.
I was hoping that I would have heard more alternatives from the hon. members who spoke in this debate. They gave one alternative, namely, to mothball. Is that the way to run the country? If you have alternatives that will benefit the country, give them. Give some alternatives which will help the minister make a good decision. Do not come up with just one alternative solution, such as to mothball the project. If we ran the country in that manner we would really be in a mess.
You are.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I would like to inform the hon. member for Vaudreuil that when the original motion was transferred for debate, officials within the Department of Transport were already in the process of readying the documentation requested for tabling in the House.

May 13, 1982
Airport Services
In conclusion, I would like to stress upon the hon. members that most of the information compiled as a result of this study is already public knowledge. The positions of the air carriers with respect to any transfer of traffic to Mirabel have been made public in a news release by the Air Transport Association of Canada. I have a copy of it here. It was released as far back as April 22, 1981, under the heading, "ATAC statement on Pepin's Dorval Mirabel options". It says:
ATAC believes that one of the two options, i.e., the transfer of all air traffic, except short-haul domestic flights, from Dorval to Mirabel, would result in higher costs and great inconvenience to travellers; would impose serious new financial burdens on financially fragile airlines, and would require unwarranted major expenditures of public money that should not be countenanced by any prudent government or responsible M.P.
Do you agree?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The hon. member asks if I agree. I do not think the minister has, at this point, taken one side or the other. That is why I was hoping this debate would have produced various alternatives, which I could have taken to him.
Individual air carriers have, on several occasions, stated their position with respect to any changes in the assignment of traffic at Montreal. One needs only to pick up any newspaper, such as the The Gazette dated April 28, which has the headline "Air giants face new pressure to move to Mirabel". Another article is headed, "Mirabel shift would raise air fares". Mr. Taylor, in a speech to the Montreal Chamber of Commerce, said that while Mirabel has the potential to become one of the world's great airports, any further transfers of traffic from Dorval to Mirabel would be economically unsound at this time for both airlines and travellers.
I do not know what the intent of the member for Vaudreuil was in making a motion for the production of papers. Really, people's positions are quite well known. All you have to do is to read the newspapers.
Furthermore, one needs only to pick up any issue of a Montreal daily newspaper to read about some particular group being either in favour of or opposed to a particular scenario for allocating traffic between the two airports.
As I have stated previously in the House, the Mirabel-Dorval solution must be one that recognizes the long-term socio-economic development of the Montreal area. There can be no doubt about the importance of proper airport facilities to the economic wellbeing of a community. Such a solution can only be found, however, after all the facts have been thoroughly assessed.
Given the rapidly changing times and the unstable world economic situation, such an assessment is not easily made, and consequently a decision on this issue will only be forthcoming at such time as the minister is confident that the best solution has been determined and that he has been able to convince his cabinet colleagues accordingly.
I would like to take this opportunity to thank the hon. member for Vaudreuil for raising this topic because it gave hon. members who were interested in it the opportunity to give
their views and state alternative solutions. My only disappointment was that I wish I had heard more alternatives and possible solutions which I could have taken to my minister.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make on the construction of Mirabel Airport. There was, of course, the initial decision to build this airport. I also want to comment on the positive impact of the airport and also on the less favourable effect it has had on the airport facilities at Dorval. During the 1960s, the growth of air transportation in Canada was tremendous, especially in flights to Europe and North America. Air transportation progressed annually at rates varying from 8 per cent to 15 per cent, and as a result, it was necessary to expand all our major airports. Increased air traffic at Dorval, and especially the advent of jet planes for long-haul flights, created a serious conflict between the need to expand operations and the fact that people in the surrounding areas were suffering increasing exposure to the noise connected with airport operations so that it became necessary to restrict-operating hours. Towards the end of the 1960s, the alternative was to either acquire new property and expand Dorval or select another site that would eventually replace Dorval.
It was thought at the time that the first solution would permanently add to the problems of surrounding communities, because the noise factor could only be expected to increase. It seemed more sensible to opt for the second alternative, namely to develop a new site that would minimize the environmental impact. The share of air traffic originally proposed in 1975 for Mirabel consisted of international flights other than those to the United States, while long-haul flights to western Canada would necessarily be directed to Mirabel.
Now to the present situation. Following consultations with Canadian carriers, only international flights have been transferred, because the airlines maintain it is impractical to fragment domestic traffic. Here I would like to mention the positive impact of Mirabel. It was supposed to eliminate congestion at Dorval in the air terminal, on the runways and the roads to and from the airport. There would also be a substantial reduction in noise near Dorval, and more than 2,500 jobs would be created in the area north of Montreal. The road network would be considerably improved as a result of the construction of the longest section of Highway 13, installation of street lighting along Highway 15 and improvement of regional and local roads. There would be no restriction on air operations at Mirabel.
Hon. members will agree that there was a great deal to be said in favour of opening a new airport at Mirabel. Obviously, there is also a negative side which concerns the airport facilities in Montreal and the decline in the level of service provided to passengers in transit in Montreal, who often have to travel between Dorval and Mirabel. This may be resulting in a loss of traffic. There is also the fact that more time and increased costs are involved for passengers who have to use Mirabel.
May 13, 1982

Obviously, the problems encountered by air carriers who had to use both airports led to other decisions, and most of the negative effects would be relatively short-lived, since the original traffic transfer plan provided that in 1975 Mirabel would be taking over the majority of Montreal's flights, except for short-haul flights. However, slow growth of air traffic owing to various economic and social problems, the financial situation of the airlines and the opposition of some groups in the Montreal Urban Community have all in some respect contributed to the postponing of a decision in this respect. The issue has been studied thoroughly for several years. There is, however, a risk of promoting solutions that would merely reinforce the negative aspects of the traffic split.
Several scenarios for traffic sharing have been considered, but there are only one or two that would meet the main objective which is to give Montreal efficient airport facilities while helping to develop transportation, supporting the economic viability of carriers and providing a comprehensive and efficient service to the travelling public. One of the most controversial aspects of increased utilization of Mirabel is surface transportation, in terms of access time, additional costs and road congestion. A number of experts have examined these factors, especially road congestion, and since some conclusions have been received, I shall mention the main ones. It is true that for many travellers it takes longer and is more expensive to go to Mirabel than to Dorval. However, the travelling time to Mirabel compares favourably with the situation in other major air traffic centres such as New York, Paris, Rome or London, to name a few. Actually, the express bus service provided by the MUCTC from downtown Montreal is fast- about fifty minutes-and very comfortable.
Other options were considered, including railway transportation that could provide a better service, and the conclusions of these studies were that a high-speed train that would make the trip from Mirabel to Montreal in thirty-five minutes would require the construction of a new tunnel under Montreal at a cost of several hundred million dollars. This option was therefore rejected. The second option, a semi-high-speed train, which would take forty to forty-five minutes and use the present tunnel under Mount Royal and existing railway tracks, would still cost more than $100 million in 1980 dollars. The possibility of a semi-high-speed train is still being considered, but it is a fact that the infrastructure costs are relatively high compared to that of a bus line. Also, the service is not that much quicker that the present bus service. According to the experience at a number of other airports, there is no marked preference for trains and the majority of travellers still prefer to go by car.
Actually, the road system from downtown to Mirabel and the restricted-access roads from Mirabel to downtown Montreal are fairly good. Once Highway 13 is completed, this will cut down even more on travelling time. Of course, completion of this highway was promised by other levels of government, and it seems that it has not been completed as planned. Mr. Airport Services
Speaker, in concluding, I wish to say that construction of a railway line would require a high passenger volume to be profitable, and would not be justified unless the volume of passenger traffic increases very substantially over the one existing at the present time. The train as such will not generate additional traffic. The surface aspect is only one of the factors that adds to the complexity of the analysis. Clearly, any decision will have to make a thorough assessment of all these factors. I shall conclude with the comment that there are not many alternatives, and I feel that in the House, most of the options-if there were any and I do not see very many, Mr. Speaker-were often presented in a very partisan spirit and often failed to consider the interests of the majority of our fellow citizens.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to what my colleagues had to say about Mirabel Airport, but none of the hon. members who spoke to this subject this afternoon were here when the decision was announced in 1969. I was one of the members in this House at that time, and I must say that the decision, and it was a long-term decision, was made after lengthy consideration and many in-depth studies. When I hear my colleagues opposite saying that the airport should be mothballed or should be split in two to send some of it to Ottawa and Washington, I must say there is only one step from the sublime to the ridiculous. Usually, people who take the shorter view of things are on the opposite side of the House, and in fact that is why they are in the opposition. People with a more realistic view of the future are usually on the government side. And when a government becomes a shortsighted government, it does not take long for it to land in the opposition. In the case of Mirabel, Mr. Speaker, 1 feel this was one of the best decisions ever made by a federal government since Confederation. It is certainly the best decision ever made for Quebec.
As a parliamentarian, I have had an opportunity to visit a number of countries and I have travelled to several airports throughout the world. I must say that Mirabel compares very favourably with any of these. In Toronto, for instance, if you have to change planes, very often you have to take a minibus and transfer to another air terminal, which may take half an hour or an hour. This is never mentioned. If you go to Paris, you have to change airports. If you go to New York, you have to change airports and it takes hours, and hundreds of millions of dollars just go down the drain. If you go to Mirabel, you do not have to change air terminals. You do not even have to walk to the plane. So there are very real advantages, and all foreigners arriving at Mirabel are amazed at the size of the airport and the surrounding area. It has been much criticized, but I still think this was one of the wisest decisions ever made. I know that some parliamentarians are talking about giving back part of the land. I think that would be a serious mistake.

May 13, 1982
Taxation
Once more, I believe these people take the shorter view and have an entirely mistaken concept of the future. I think that people who talk about mothballing Mirabel are talking through their hats. I heard one of my colleagues from the Progressive Conservative Party say that the best farmland in Quebec was used for this airport, although it is widely known that most of the land, although excellent farmland, was not under cultivation, and that today, farm production, despite the construction of Mirabel Airport, has increased over what it was in 1969. These things are forgotten because there is no knowledge of the real situation. Mr. Speaker, I could go on for two hours about Mirabel. When they talk about it, all they can say is that you need a taxi and it costs $40 to get there. As my colleague said, Highway 13 has not been completed. Three years ago, the federal government signed an agreement with Quebec for the completion of this highway.

speechtext:
I guess the Vancouver Canucks are going to be playing hockey tonight. I surmise that is the reason for the waving of one of their sweaters.
Prior to private members' hour, I was expressing the thought that it was unbelievable that a cabinet or a government could be as incompetent as the one which brought in the National Energy Program which is causing destruction of the economic wellbeing of this country. There is no doubt about it. We have
never had a program which has done as much damage to this country as has the National Energy Program. The people who perpetrated it will not listen.
I should state tonight that it is a pleasure not only to speak on behalf of my constituents, but to do so also on behalf of those of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) who is looking after the people's interest in another part of the country. Our problems are pretty much the same. 1 am sure he would support anything that I say in trying to bring the attention of this government to the serious problems it is creating for Canadians.
The heavy hand of government is taking more and more of the gross national product in taxes. The figure is creeping up each year. Unfortunately, the government does not seem prepared to cut the pattern to fit the cloth. On a national accounts basis, expenditures for all levels of government which far exceed receipts of most years, are inching up to almost one half the GNP. In 1977, government expenditures accounted for 41.4 per cent of the GNP. In 1978, the last complete year for which the Canadian Tax Foundation has provided information, government spending accounted for 42 per cent of GNP. This year the percentage will be that much worse because the GNP is growing much more slowly and government expenditures are escalating more rapidly.
As the Canadian Tax Foundation notes, such payments, which include pensions, family allowances, unemployment insurance railway subsidies and interest on the public debt, redistribute income within the economy but do not increase the government's claim on the goods and services produced. That is a gentle way of saying that government is passing out dollars it has not produced, and the net result is that no new wealth or productivity is created.
Government taxes take about 38 per cent of the gross national product, that is government at ail levels, and the federal government takes the lion's share, a share almost equal to the combined share taken by the two other levels of government.
Federal tax collections amounted to only 7 per cent of GNP in 1926. They peaked at 21 per cent in 1946 and then rose to 30.5 per cent in 1978. Together with revenue from other sources, capital cost allowances, investment income and other minor items totalling 7.7 per cent, a hefty 38.1 per cent was taken out of the gross national product.
My own province of Alberta shells out $5,028 billion in all forms of taxes to Ottawa and gets back $3,490 billion. That means we are a net loser to the tune of $1,538 billion. I guess that is the price of being a have province. However, this year there will not be the income tax coming from that province because of so many workers departing from the oil industry in Alberta. They have gone to the United States where they will be paying income tax.
May 13, 1982

I wonder how long we will continue to be a have province with this federal government's insatiable appetite for new and higher taxes. The federal government's disastrous national energy policy has wrecked the oil and gas industry in Alberta. The boom is over in Alberta thanks to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) together with their tax policy. They are the great destroyers. Their clumsy attempts to Canadianize the oil and gas industry have resulted in Americanizing it. That is where all our jobs, risk capital, drilling rigs, expertise and technology have fled. The New York Times of May 9, 1982 reported on the price of the national energy policy as follows:
Oil exploration, drilling and production plunged, prices soared and consumption fell.
New oil wells completed in 1981 were down from 8,865 the previous year to 7,165-a loss of 1,800 wells. Oil rigs in use dropped from 446 to 303-a loss of 143 rigs. Petroleum output fell from 1.76 million barrels a day to 1.61 million barrels a day. Gas prices at the pumps soared from an average of 0.61 cents a gallon in 1980 to an average of $1.21 a gallon in 1981, and up to $1.75 in 1982. Do hon. members opposite think this makes sense, when 400,000 barrels a day from Alberta is locked in?
The New York Times says that the fact is that Canada's energy policy will cut off the competitive edge in new technology just when it is most needed. What has happened since the national energy policy in Canada and Reagan decontrol in the United States? For the first time in a decade production of crude oil within the continental United States rose. Drilling of new wells increased 40 per cent and the number of operating rigs hit a record high. Matching this increase, continued decreases in per capita consumption caused crude imports to decline by as much as half a million barrels a day.
The New York Times went on to say that in Canada, on the other hand, 1981 production of crude oil and natural gas fell 10 per cent and 4 per cent respectively. Exploratory activities declined by 20 per cent in western Canada as companies moved to the north to obtain production incentive payments or left the country entirely.
The article in The New York Times said that while $4 billion to $5 billion was spent on drilling, $7 billion left Canada as Canadian companies bought out foreign interests. The outlook is for another 25 per cent reduction in well completions this year. Thus, more than half the rigs in the country during 1980 will have left by the end of 1982, principally for the United States.
So much for the Canadianization of our industry. And The New York Times concluded:
If the northern projects fail, as the $13 billion Alsands heavy-oil project did, then Canada will be importing half of its crude oil by the end of the decade. Since the United States should only be importing 10 per cent of its crude by that time, the Canadians will likely come to us for help in the next embargo. Let us not be of assistance, given that they've wrecked their markets and expelled efficient United States companies. Let them freeze in the dark.
Taxation
That is a sad commentary the United States has made about the activities of this government. There is no remorse among members opposite, and there does not seem to be any understanding.
So much for our goal of energy self-sufficiency by the end of this decade. If Sir Wilfrid Laurier were alive, do you think he might say that the twenty-first century will belong to Canada, and the twenty-second? Canadian individuals and industries are being buried by taxation, they are being frustrated by new and revised levies. The Fraser Institute on the west coast said, in a recent report:
In 1961, for example, the average family had an income of $5,000 and faced a total tax bill of $1,675.00; by 1980, the average family was earning $22,500 but of that $10,306 went to the tax collectors at the federal and provincial municipal levels in the form of hidden and direct taxes. The Institute's tax index shows that the tax bill of the average family has increased by 515 per cent since 1961.
In fact, it has increased even more in recent years because of the increasing extent to which governments, especially the federal government, have engaged in deficit financing. The bonds that governments issue to cover these deficits are, in effect, deferred taxation, since tax revenue must ultimately be raised to pay the interest and redeem the bonds. Including this deferred taxation, the Fraser Institute estimates that taxes between 1961 and 1980 have gone up 619 per cent. I wonder if in this reconciliation of net debt, this so-called deferred taxation, the Fraser Institute has taken into consideration the billions and billions of dollars the government owes for Crown corporation debts and the pension and superannuation funds.
And then, of course, we heard the member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) saying today that he did not mind the government buying oil companies, companies that do not produce another barrel of oil, and the money leaving Canada in large amounts.
The last public accounts of 1980-81 show that the government has to account for $18.9 billion in Canada pension at 10.59 per cent. Does the government have that money? The accounts also show $22.3 billion in public service pension contributions at 8.2 per cent, $8.7 billion in the Canadian Armed Forces superannuation fund, which it does not have, and almost $1 billion in the RCMP retirement fund.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I know that this is of concern to you, because we have sat on many committees and discussed this. I was absolutely flabbergasted, when I was elected as a Member of Parliament, to find that these funds did not exist. It actually is a paper debt that the federal government owes to all these people. No other business in the world would be allowed to do this. If that money existed in those funds, it would be different, but it does not. It is a debt the government owes to the Canadian people.
Those are liabilities of the government, which simply show up in the public accounts as specified purpose accounts. As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, this adds up to almost $51 billion, just in those three or four accounts alone. Then, of course, we have people on the other side-elected representatives of the people, saying it is okay to go on buying oil companies.
80114 31

May 13, 1982
Taxation
Taxes today account for a more significant chunk of the consumer budget than shelter and food combined. The average family with a $22,500 income paid $10,305 in all taxes and had average shelter costs of $4,239 and average food costs of $4,631, for a total of $8,870.
The Fraser Institute said: "In other words, taxes other than incomes taxes accounted for nearly 70 per cent of the total tax bill of the average Canadian family." And many of these taxes were hidden taxes. Commenting on the Fraser Institute report, the St. John's Evening Telegram editorialized:
Most Canadians, unfortunately, won't see a copy of this Fraser Institute document, and they will scarcely get such information from their taxman or their political representatives. But, until they "wise up" to the fact that governments cannot spend the people's money better than the people themselves, we will continue on the long slide to total dependency on the state and its expensive bureaucracy.
The Calgary Herald said in an editorial:
Nevertheless, there is a point at which any further increase in the proportion of total income taken through taxes is held to be intolerable. That point may vary from time to time according to the perceived worthiness of governmental programs and performance, but it is out there somewhere and governments dare not ignore it.
If they do so, they do so at their own peril.
The message of the Fraser Institute's report is that the point of intolerance is substantially closer today than it was in 1961 and that further appreciable increases in taxation, relative to real wealth, may be at the risk of economic wellbeing and political stability.
The escalation in energy prices has had a drastic effect on the food chain. I must impress upon this House, Mr. Speaker, that it is not necessarily the escalation in the price of energy that is creating the problems, but, rather, it is the taxation of the energy. Farmers must pay higher prices for their energy and for their products which have a high energy concentration, such as, for example, fertilizer. These costs must be passed on, and eventually they come to roost at the checkout counters in the supermarkets.
I have here a document from one of my constituents which shows that the tax on natural gas alone is creating real hardships for many people. One fairly large hog operation in my constituency had a tax bill of $725.95 for the month of March alone. That was just excise tax on natural gas alone. That is more than the total cost at the original installation, so we can see the devastating effect of this excise tax on natural gas. This has to be added to the cost of the operation, and that cost is reflected right through to the grocery counter. The consumer will have to pay. We should not be taxing fuel for home heating or fuel used in production because that is where Canada is falling down.
I also have a letter from Mr. Gerald Kemp, who is a director of the Federated Co-operatives Limited. He is also the vicepresident in the Calgary region. This is what he wrote to me:
The following is an excerpt from a directive sent through Federated Cooperatives Limited-
"There is concern among agricultural producers over the effect that scheduled increases in energy costs, as negotiated in the Canada-Alberta energy agreement, will have on farm production costs. While we are sympathetic to the need for higher energy costs, we share the concern of producers. Based on the projected
increases to the cost of crude oil and natural gas, we have calculated the effect these will have on a farm with 1,000 acres under cultivation. The cost of motor fuel, heating fuel, and fertilizer for such an operation was about $11,820 in 1980, and increased to $16,573 in 1981. Our calculations indicate that by 1986, costs will increase to about $42,536, an increase of 280 per cent over the 1980 level. The predictable result is that as well as eroding farm income, the increased costs will be reflected in the food bill for all families".
He included working papers. Motor fuel for that farm with
1,000	acres under cultivation in 1980 cost $4,540; heating fuel cost $810; fertilizer cost $6,470, for a total of $ 11,820. Then in 1981 the motor fuel cost $6,860; heating fuel cost $1,223; and fertilizer cost $8,670. The total was up to $16,753. In 1986 we will find that from $16,753 the cost will go up to $42,536.
How in the world are these people going to survive and keep producing if the government continues to impose taxes like these on the industry? It just cannot be done. There is absolutely no way those people can survive. The government must realize that one third of the cost of natural gas is federal tax. In addition to that, the federal government will not wait for the tax to be collected by the co-operatives. No, it has to have it within 30 days. There is absolutely no way co-operatives can collect the tax and pay it to the federal treasury in 30 days. They need 90 days. But no, the government will not listen. Not only does the federal government take approximately one third of the cost of natural gas in tax, but there is also a top loading because the tax must be financed for 60 days. A co-operative has to have about $100,000 at any one given period, and that is borrowed from the bank. These co-operatives have to pay ordinary interest, so hon. members can imagine the extra cost involved. It is absolutely senseless that we have allowed ourselves to get into that kind of situation.
The escalation in energy prices has had drastic effects on the food chain, and it will have a much worse effect in the future.
The cost of air travel is becoming prohibitive. Because of the massive VIA Rail cuts, that is the only option left to some communities. Last May the government introduced the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge to force air carriers to pay world prices for fuel used in international flights. The initial levy was about 11 cents a litre. The government used this dodge because it claimed that foreign carriers were taking advantage of cheap Canadian gas prices to tanker fuel from this country. The airlines, through the Air Transport Association of Canada, fought this measure, claiming it was simply an illegal export tax on fuel. They said it was discriminatory because it applied only to aviation jet and marine fuel. They said it contravened bilateral air agreements and that it was never made into law. Air Canada, Nordair and a couple of other airlines paid, but other Canadian carriers withheld their payments pending the outcome of protests. Foreign carriers all paid the illegal levy. Canada caved in when the United States got tough and threatened to take the levy to international arbitration. The recovery charge ended on January 31. The foreign carriers, who paid a total of $46.5 million, can apply for a rebate. The $50 million paid or owed by Canadian carriers will not be rebated, and the Canadian consumer does not get a rebate either.
May 13, 1982

Foreign carriers will get a break. British Airways will get back $4.5 million. Canadian Pacific owes $11.5 million. The new scheme to get around the recovery charge boggles the mind, but it amounts to the same thing. Canadian carriers have to keep separate accounts for fuel used on domestic and international flights. The Air Transport Association of Canada believes that this sneaky scheme is also illegal, and it is deciding whether to challenge it in court. It is a monumental rip-off of the domestic airlines and is resulting in higher costs in fares for travellers. Canada must surely be the only country in the world where domestic carriers are singled out for special punishment in the form of irregular and doubtful energy levies.
In the end who pays? It is the Canadian consumer who pays, and no one else. It is terribly difficult to understand why the elected officials of the people on the side of the House opposite me would stand idly by and let three people, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister get away with it.
The late John Diefenbaker had a phrase for this. He used to call the rare affliction most Liberals have the "Otto Lang syndrome." Mr Diefenbaker used to say in the House that if Otto Lang was walking across a cow pasture with four cow pies in it, he would walk in all four. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources appear to have terminal cases of the disease, and the Prime Minister should put them out of their misery. I challenge hon. members across the aisle to tell me one positive benefit they have brought to Canada and Canadians in the two years plus since they were elected to office. They have brought Canada and Canadians nothing but misery. The Prime Minister shrugs and says that our economic climate is but a spin-off of worldwide recession. Nothing could be further from the truth, Mr. Speaker. As I said earlier this week in the House, he has left the Governor of the Bank of Canada hanging out to dry, trying to protect the Canadian dollar with high interest rates. He forgets that the gross national product and the fiscal responsibility of the government adds more to the protection of the Canadian dollar than interest rates ever could.
The statements of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance are just baloney. We are in poor shape because the economy is being mismanaged. Every major economic indicator is in disarray. The Liberals achieved office through stealth and guile. They lied to the Canadian people when they said that they would keep the increase in the price of gasoline below 18 cents per gallon and probably at around 14 cents, to quote the Prime Minister. There have been about 15 gas and oil price increases since the Liberals were returned to office, but some of these were due to the extra taxes that were levied. How can they justify this when they were returned to office on a promise of keeping prices down?
In 1981 a typical Canadian family driving one car and heating their home with oil paid about $550 more per year
Taxation
than in late 1980. Of this, $409 was paid indirectly to the federal government.
Since the Liberals assumed office in 1980 the cost of heating a home has just about doubled. Where the average annual cost was about $560 in 1979, the cost in the winter of 1981-82 was just about double that. I have never had so many complaints from people about the cost of heating their homes. Senior citizens have to pay $100 to $125 more to heat their homes. They used to be able to heat them for $25 or $30.
The price of natural gas for home heating was driven up by excessive federal taxation. One third of that cost is federal tax and goes directly into federal revenues. Two years ago there was no excise tax on natural gas for home heating. Now the consumer pays about 32 per cent of the total cost in the form of excise taxes to the federal government.
Not content with avoiding cow flaps, this accident prone government is spending its spare time creating new cow flaps to walk in. We wasted a year and a half on the Constitution, a pet project of the Prime Minister. The debate was counterproductive and divisive and did nothing to draw this nation closer together or to increase productivity and real growth. We ended up with a flawed document, which will be a judicial nightmare and a bonanza only for lawyers.
We could have used all that time to ensure that proper procedures were developed for the tarsands. Cancellation of the megaprojects is a body blow to the Canadian economy, and in particular to the province of Alberta. At a time when we need productivity and jobs, we are being forced deeper and deeper into the morass of recession and despair. I have never seen the morale of the Canadian people as low as it is today.
Canadians have been browbeaten and put down for too long. They need hope, they need optimism and they need confidence in their elected officers and their elected leaders. They need a government which, first of all, understands what makes our marketplace economy tick.
The government says it wants to nationalize the Canadian energy industry. I say that for the word "nationalize" it should substitute the word "socialize" because that is what it is trying to do. Its clumsy attempts to Canadianize the industry have resulted in an Americanization of the industry. That is where all our drilling rigs are-in the United States. That is where about $17 billion in risk capital, equipment and payroll has fled. Mr. Bouey is left trying to protect the outflow of the Canadian dollar with high interest rates, when it is being shovelled out the back door faster than it is coming in the front.
The little independent businessman, the service and supply small businessman, is feeling the squeeze most in Alberta. Companies have gone under. Operations have been transferred to the United States. Jobs have been lost. Most people out there thought that the future looked bright for them. They invested their life earnings, and much of that has disappeared.
The ripple effect has spread into the manufacturing plants in Quebec and Ontario. There is no way of telling just what the loss of activity in the oil patch means to the steel mills and

May 13, 1982
Taxation
auto plants in central Canada. I dare say that the impact has been devastating. Companies in Alberta are not buying the cars or trucks that they would ordinarily buy, and this is reflected in the eastern market.
I am normally an optimistic person, Mr. Speaker, but I fear for my country. I fear because there are men across the aisle who do not know what they are doing, nor do they seem to care. I fear for my country because the clumsy, ham-handed, bumbling of the government is fueling the fires of separation and separatist talk and action in the provinces.
I fear for my Canada because there are more than a million Canadians without jobs and unable to find work. I fear for my Canada because for many the dream of owning their homes has vanished in the smoke of high interest rates and double digit inflation. I fear for my Canada because the government is doing nothing to stimulate the economy. It has done nothing for productivity, for industrial strategy, for research and development. We had the promise of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) that if interest rates increased he would resign, but he is still with us, Mr. Speaker.
We are still hewers of wood and drawers of water, Mr. Speaker. Dr. Larkin Kerwin, President of the National Research Council, says that the Japanese do so much with so little and we do so little with so much! It is tragic, when the potential is there for greatness and for prosperity.
Laurier said that the twentieth century would belong to Canada. May we expect a statement from the right hon. gentleman amending Laurier's prediction? Will we perhaps hear him say that the twenty-first century will belong to Canada, or maybe the twenty-second century?
We have been content for too long to let the external forces of world patterns and conditions pull and tug us along. We have been passive instruments, not active movers, shakers and doers.
It is the responsibility of the government to establish the climate in which all this can be brought about, Mr. Speaker, and we hold it responsible. If it cannot achieve this then it should resign and let someone do the job who can.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was shocked to hear how members of the opposition described the national energy policy, which was agreed to by the western provinces through negotiation and compromise on all sides. A lot of Canadians may fail to realize that under the terms of the British North America Act and the new Constitution it is recognized that resources within a province come under provincial jurisdiction. When a product crosses a provincial or international boundary, however, it comes within the jurisdiction of the federal government. It is in these areas that an agreement had to be worked out between the producing provinces and the federal government.
I want to make it plain, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government does not set retail prices. It establishes the price paid by refiners for crude, however; that is, the blended price. As of January 1, 1982, this stands at 70.6 per cent of world
price. After a refinery purchases the crude at the blended price, several costs are added to the retail price, such as the cost of refining and of transportation to market. Profit margins for refiners and retailers are often influenced by local competition. And retail sales taxes, a constant 9 per cent for federal taxes, but from zero to 40 per cent for provincial taxes in the case of gasoline. There is no provincial tax on gasoline in Alberta, but in the province of Quebec it amounts to 40 per cent. The breakdown of federal government taxes is 0.72 cents per litre of gasoline for the Canadian ownership charge, with which we have purchased Petrofina, which will be paid for this coming fall. The sales tax is 2.40 cents a litre. The excise tax is 1.5 cents. The upstream tax, including federal corporation tax, is 2.79 cents a litre. The total federal tax per litre of gasoline is 7.41 cents.
