speechtext: Would the hon. member entertain a very short question?

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
At the end of my statement, Mr. Speaker.
I would also like to point out that the petroleum compensation charge returns to the industry. Perhaps Ontario has gone up to 40 per cent in their new budget, but before six o'clock tonight the province of Ontario took 16 per cent, the Government of Canada took 18.8 per cent, and the producing provinces had 12.3 per cent. However, the industry had 42.9 per cent of a litre of gasoline. Add the petroleum compensation charge to the 42.9 per cent, and that would appear to be a very logical division of income from that litre of gasoline that retailed at 39.1 cents per litre.
Getting back to the agreement arrived at last September, it was agreed that, subject to the fiscal undertakings contained in the agreement, it was the intention of the government to set the rate of the petroleum and gas revenue tax at 16 per cent effective January 1, 1982. There would be provision for a 25 per cent resource allowance, and then an incremental oil revenue tax at a rate of 50 per cent on incremental old oil revenues after deduction of related Crown royalties. I wish to point out that in many of the provinces those royalties ran as high as 21 per cent. In the province I come from, where we own our mineral rights, those royalties are 12.5 per cent. For one of the Indian bands which appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs a year ago in March, the royalties averaged 60 per cent. So when we talk about the need for royalties to be reduced, particularly on low producing wells, the need is there. The Government of Canada recognized this because it made an adjustment in its incremental oil revenue tax to compensate for this. This assistance came into effect January 1, 1982, and is known as the low productivity well allowance. It applies to wells which produce less than 3.18 cubic metres of oil per day, or less than 20 barrels. That arose from the comprehensive energy agreements reached with the producing provinces in the fall of 1981. I believe, if my figures are correct, that this will apply to approximately 40 per cent of wells in Alberta and may account
May 13, 1982

for about 10 per cent of the oil produced. It will apply to most of the wells in my own riding, which are very small but very important.
I would suggest that in the administration of this tax there is a need for an agreement with the producers on wells operating in one central collection system, wells which are still in existence today. There should be a special allowance made so that one common gathering tank can be used to collect the oil, and the tax should then be applied on the total, and averaged out over the total number of wells. Some of these wells are more than 100 years old and maybe they are only producing one, two or three barrels a day. It is a very expensive proposition to have a collection tank for each one of these wells, but working out a single system of collection and bookkeeping to administer the tax will be a big help. I have already made submissions to the minister in this regard and he has looked upon them very favourably. I suggest these taxes are not out of line when you consider what is being paid in other countries by the oil industry.
Looking back in history, the North American petroleum industry as it is known today did not begin in Texas or in Pennsylvania; it began in Eastern Canada, my own area. The technology spread into other areas of Canada and around the world. But they had their problems, too. It was back in the late 1800s and the early 1900s that drillers from my constituency went into 70 different countries in the world with their technology to produce the oil. The irony of it was that within a very few years the price of oil tumbled drastically and a lot of those old wells in my area were shut down because of the flood of cheap oil hitting the market, particularly from the United States. The potential is still there because even the fields discovered back in the 1850s still contain approximately 60 per cent of the oil originally discovered. So it is a very positive move on the part of the minister to ensure that the low producing wells had a special tax incentive to allow them to extract the rest of that oil. Perhaps as this is applied to Alberta a lot of the service rigs will go back to work bringing these wells back into productivity.
In listening to the previous speakers, I could not help thinking that theirs is a typical response. I should remind the hon. member across the floor that it was not the federal government which made the production cuts last year which resulted in the increase of oil imports. I would like to make a couple of comparisons. For example, the 1981 annual report of Amoco Canada says:
The federal government's National Energy Program, announced in late 1980, was primarily responsible for a near one-third reduction in both the company's 1981 net income and cash flow. Subsequently, the long-awaited pricing and revenue sharing agreements concluded between Ottawa and Alberta in September, 1981, did very little to improve the company's financial performance. Moreover, the Alberta crude oil production cutbacks, imposed during the ... negotiations, seriously reduced our production during the year. The after-effects of these cutbacks were continuing to impact on our production beyond year end.
The amazing part of the entire report is that drilling and exploratory activities from 1977 until 1981 showed a success ratio which increased from 32.6 per cent to 44 per cent. That was a tremendous increase in the success ratio. Also it is
Taxation
amazing that while total exploratory wells drilled were down in 1981, extension and development wells in oil producing sectors nearly doubled in 1981 over 1980. They knew where that oil was, so those were the wells they developed. They developed seven wells in 1980 compared with 13.9 wells in 1981. Their net oil wells increased by 50 wells. By December 31, 1981, there were 901 oil wells, compared with 851 wells in 1980.
Turning to page 15 of the annual report of Imperial Oil, it shows that in 1980 the company had an interest in 35 wells drilled in Canada, and that in 1981 it had an interest in 44 wells, for an increase of nine wells. These were exploration wells to determine the location of oil fields. However, we know that there was a decrease in gas well development. I can understand this because of the thousands of shut-in gas wells in Alberta currently. There is no market for the gas, so they are capped. It is only logical, consequently, that they would concentrate their development in oil producing areas, especially when there is a surplus of natural gas. Perhaps the most telling statement, when we look at the annual reports and compare them, can be found in the 1981 annual report of Imperial Oil. It was the statement of the retiring chairman of the board and chief executive officer, Mr. J. A. Armstrong, in which he said:
The industry is passing through a period of transition but Canada, almost alone among industrialized nations, possesses the opportunity for achieving selfsufficiency in all forms of energy within the foreseeable future. And it is energy development, more than any other industrial activity, that offers Canada the greatest prospects for economic growth. For a resource-rich country in a resource-hungry world, energy development represents a major opportunity and a major priority. And hydrocarbon development, for obvious reasons, heads the list.
The federal government certainly recognizes the importance of energy development to Canada's future. Its growing role in the petroleum industry is to be expected at a time when oil supply has become a matter of national concern. Imperial, for its part, supports many of the objectives contained in the federal government's National Energy Program, in particular the achievement of selfsufficiency in oil.
He was very emphatic that Imperial Oil supports many of these programs. He continued:
And moreover, we have never been opposed to the intent of the program in promoting greater Canadian ownership of the oil industry. It is entirely reasonable that Canadians should play a greater role in domestic energy development.
However, it is reasonable, too, that a proper balance be struck between competing energy objectives. The urgency of energy development and the need for increased Canadian participation in that development, while both important, are very different objectives. Reconciling them represents a significant challenge for both government and industry. Canadianization will certainly reshape the oil industry and can do it in a way that benefits all Canadians.
It is very obvious that the largest of these Canadian oil companies endorses the programs of the federal government in its annual report and is prepared to proceed and expand in coordination with them.
Little more needs to be said in this regard as to the benefits of the program to all Canadians. It is the major thrust of the Government of Canada to ensure that Canadians are in charge of the energy which will shape the future of this great nation. It will allow the companies to work together, not only Imperial Oil but the other companies involved in the search for new

May 13, 1982
Taxation
resources, in a way which will benefit all of Canada and the oil industry in particular. When we look at the huge investments required in the Beaufort Sea, the Arctic, Hibernia and other offshore areas, we realize that it will take the joint efforts of a consortium to pool their resources to find new discoveries. We now have the power as a federal government to ask them to drill step-out wells which will determine the extent of the fields, so that Canadians are ensured supplies in the future.
When we look at the projections made back in the early 1970s and at the glut on the market at the present time, we realize that Canadians have a right to know and, consequently, it stands to reason that this legislation is before us in the House of Commons. It ensures that the various taxes are in place, taxes which will allow the industry to expand and to search out new areas to be developed. The present programs are different than the ones of the past.
Earlier I referred to the industry in my own area. In the town of Petrolia alone there were some 600 wells, many of which were drilled but never plugged. As they dried up, they were abandoned. That area can no longer be water-flooded or pressurized, but we must work out new schemes to recapture that old oil. Perhaps we should listen to the suggestions of one of the old pioneers who died about six weeks ago. I am referring to Mr. C. O. Fairbank, whose father once represented the Petrolia area in the House of Commons. One of his ideas was that we need to put down shafts in the shallow fields and run laterals out from there to let the oil seep in without pressurizing it.
The flexibility is in the legislation before the House. It takes into consideration the establishment of a level of tax which recognizes the need of the industry for cash flow. The industry must have adequate funds to do the job. Some activities, notably exploration, cannot be readily financed through debt alone. Either internal funding or new equity capital is needed.
Some members in the industry have suggested, however, that the oil and gas sectors must have the cash flow equal to all their projected capital investment. I find this difficult to accept because there are no compelling reasons why the industry should have such a favoured position, particularly with the returns on the investments, when the returns on the investments even this year are so attractive compared with the returns in other sectors of our economy. For example, I look at the fact that over a few years 2 per cent of that total GNP in the United States was going to the OPEC nations.
We in Canada must be certain that the climate here is as was reflected in the statement by the chairman of the board of Imperial Oil. That climate must be created in order for the Canadian companies to go ahead and expand and develop those resources here in Canada. I was delighted to read last week about the increase in value of the shares of Dome Petroleum in response to another find in the Beaufort Sea.
I would like to draw to the attention of the House that in spite of the gloom and doom that we hear from the other side regarding the megaprojects, it is not only Canada who has had
to postpone such projects. Other countries have also had to postpone projects. For example, there is the Exxon-shale project in the United States which has been stopped. In Colorado the lignite gasification program has been shelved and the panhandle coal gasification project in Wyoming has been scrapped. Mexico has delayed a huge project there, and so has Nigeria. The United Kingdom has delayed some projects in the oil field in the North Sea. The Netherlands is continuing theirs, but their emphasis is on small fields requiring a minimum financial commitment. The British Petroleum Company is turning to less costly equipment as an alternative for its North Sea development. The investment costs per barrel of oil produced is thereby being lowered.
The uncertainty of the world oil market and the pricing uncertainties have led the French to shelve plans to buy 40,000 barrels per day of heavy crude from Venezuela, as well as shelving plans to build a plant in France at a cost of over $1 billion. I suggest that even though the Alsands project has been put on hold. New technology is developing so rapidly that these plants may have been obsolete by the time they were built. Petro-Canada is very heavily involved in the experimentation and development of this new technology. I can only hope that this will continue over the next few years as the Beaufort Sea begins production along with the Hibernia oil. We know that there will be security there not only for the province of Alberta but for all of Canada, and by working together we can create the harmony which has existed since the national energy agreement was signed last September. The achievement of that agreement was a major step, as far as I am concerned, in the development of one of our primary resources that Mr. Armstrong of Imperial Oil described so well in his annual report.
Perhaps I should point out that it has been implied on many occasions that the price of gasoline may be cheaper in some parts of the United States. That may be true if one considers the level of provincial sales tax applied in Canada in various provinces, along with the federal tax. However, when these provincial sales taxes are removed or lowered to a more reasonable level there is very little difference. I would suggest that a litre of heating fuel is cheaper in Canada at the present time than it is in the United States.
I believe that we will have a much more secure future in Canada, with the energy reserves which exist in this country, if we develop them in an orderly manner.
Much has been said about equipment moving south across the border to the United States beginning in September of 1980. I want to make it clear that this exodus did not just start with the introduction of the National Energy Program on October 28, 1980. It started in September of that year. As well, many of those rigs were shallow rigs that could not achieve the depths required for the deeper fields in western Canada. There were also rigs which were left unused because of the thousands of gas wells that are capped owing to the lack of export markets.
It was interesting to note that in the last few months the activity in the United States has dropped off dramatically, and
May 13, 1982

the more modern rigs which are capable of reaching the deeper oil in Canada are beginning to return. It is also interesting to note that although some companies are suggesting that they are not renewing leases, they are in fact renewing leases in areas which have the highest potential. The reason for this is the new technology which has been developed for this.
It was only a few years ago that the seismic rigs did not have the capability of producing three dimensional readouts of the formations below the surface. This technology is now available, and I believe that the success ratio, which I referred to in the annual report earlier, demonstrates their present capabilities as compared to a few years ago. Activity is taking place in areas which show potential, and the emphasis is now being concentrated on oil production rather than on production of both gas and oil. No doubt it should be very plain to those in the oil industry and those who follow it very closely that the reason for the decrease in the over-all activity is that this activity has been stepped up in the sector of oil production itself.
I believe that the taxes proposed in the bill we are debating tonight are essential for the continuation and expansion of Canada's oil industry. It is important that the terms of the proposal are set out in the bill so that the oil companies know what lies ahead and that the provinces and the country as a whole know what is ahead of us. These taxes will benefit those Canadians in the provinces that produce oil as well as all Canadians. Taxes have to be expected by the industry involved in this sector.
1 should like to say in summary that when the industry adjusts-as Imperial Oil has shown it is doing in its annual report-and when we realize the potential which is laid out in the annual report of Petro-Canada and the reserves we have, I believe that our objectives can be achieved. This bill is a major step in the right direction.

Bill C-112 causes me great sadness because there is no doubt that Canada is in deep trouble. I will not state the statistics on unemployment, the position of our dollar or our inflation rate. There is no need to do so because Your Honour knows of them, and so do the Canadian people. But what most Canadians do not realize is that their trust in government is a misplaced trust because it is a trust which has been broken and breached by the Liberal government over some 14 years.
However, let us look at where we are. We sit here, a small number of people, 24 million, on the resources of half-continent. Other countries have huge populations and small resources. They are in trouble, and so they should be in trouble, because the vast bulk of those countries have tried this route to socialism, whether one looks at Sweden, the United Kingdom or at the ultimate in socialization, which is Russia and the East bloc. Most of those countries were wealthy countries at one time. Indeed, if one looks at Roumania, Poland or Russia, one finds that they were exporters of food until they became socialized, which simply means that the decisions are made by a small group of people.
That is what the National Energy Program does. It takes that huge oil industry which we had, where millions of individual decisions were made throughout the course of the year, where there was instant adaptability to changing climate, circumstances and finance in the world and all the other items of change, and it brings that decision-making to Ottawa. We now have a small cabinet which is really inundated with so many other concerns that it honestly cannot make those decisions, and we also have a bureaucracy which is totally isolated from the reality of the world. Those people in the cabinet are making decisions. Of course, it has not worked in any other country in the world, and it will not work here.

speechtext: Well, they have been. Why has the Canadian ownership charge gone up so much? Why do we have 400 Crown corporations? Let me tell Your Honour why Crown corporations do not work. speechtext:
What is your position on Petro-Canada this week? Are you for it or against it?
May 13, 1982

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The hon. member opposite speaks about Petro-Canada. There is no doubt that it will succeed. It will succeed if it has to take every last tax dollar out of every last Canadian's pocket. As the last speaker said, they will not do away with that tax. They will purchase another company. They must take away all private companies because they set up a competitive position which makes Petro-Canada look sick.
We have over $2 billion in Petro-Canada, and it cannot make it on the open market. If we were not kicking in $400 million a year and $800 million for the purchase of Petrofina, PetroCan would be gone. It cannot compete. It would not be able to compete if we were in government. It does not matter which is the label of the government. It is just an inefficiency that is inappropriate, particularly in the oil and gas industry.
The Canadian people will learn a lesson in the co-operative movement. The government has offered to the co-operative movement $100 million if it will kick in some money and set up a co-operative oil and gas company. I predict with absolute certainty that the members of a co-op will suffer a terrible loss.
The oil industry is not like the airline industry to which you give routes. All it has to do is to buy some planes, put some people on them and fly back and forth. You can do away with competition, as was done with Air Canada.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: What about Pacific Western?

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Canadian Pacific cannot get in. They can make it work, but the oil and gas industry depends on people with creativity, people who are prepared to work 18 and 20 hours a day. You do not get that in a Crown corporation. Members opposite can laugh, but I am confident that in a few months or years Canadians will come to realize that.
I want to deal with some comments made by previous speakers. The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) seemed to imply that the producing provinces totally agreed to all of the provisions in the agreement which they signed and therefore were in favour of the federal taxes. That simply is not the case. The province of Alberta had a position to protect its citizens in their capacity as owners of the resource. The federal government had a position to protect what it thought was the national interest. They negotiated and ultimately came to an agreement. Albertans were party to that agreement only to the extent of protecting Albertans as owners of the resource and were in no way condoning all the federal taxes.
They really had no choice because the federal government had unilaterally come out with a National Energy Program which said it would do this and this and this. The provinces had no choice because under the Constitution the federal government was really intruding into provincial jurisdiction. For example, these taxes were put on as a royalty, so the provinces had no choice but to defend themselves. That led to a stalemate. Months and months passed, and finally a mutual agreement was reached under which the citizens of Alberta
Taxation
were satisfied with the royalty portion they were keeping. That does not imply they were in favour of the federal taxes.
The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex pointed out that the blended price is now 70.6 per cent of the world price. Canadians now pay 70 per cent of the world price to the owners of the resource, but the retail price is much higher than in the United States. In the United States, they give the owners 100 per cent of the world price, and yet their retail price is less than ours. The difference, of course, is in the taxation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: It is provincial.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: There is no tax in Alberta or Saskatchewan.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I know my facts. If the backbenchers on the other side had been doing their job for their constituents, they would know the facts. The difference is in taxes, provincial and federal, which means that Canadians are paying more.
In the United States there is an excess profits tax. If the world price goes up and the cost of producing the resource does not, there is an excess profit which the U.S. government taxes away to the benefit of its citizens. When the world price drops and there is less profit, there is less tax. We have not chosen to do that in Canada. We have a fixed tax. Whether the price is up or down, a Canadian citizen must continue to pay that price. That is why our retail price is more than in the United States.
Let me give an example. In Ontario the price per gallon was recently $1.67. Of that, 22 cents went to the people of Alberta as owners of the resource. That was the royalty, 22 cents. The Ontario government took 25 cents by way of a tax. The people of Ontario and other provinces need to know that their provincial governments are taxing oil and gas being sold at the pumps. That 25 cents is more than the owners receive, an interesting point.
Let us look at the federal tax. Why is the federal government taxing the purchaser 53 cents on a gallon of gas which sells for $1.67? That is regressive tax. That is not part of the progressive income tax system where the rich pay more than the poor. When you put a tax on a gallon of gas of 57 cents, it hurts the poor much more than those of us with a higher income.
The federal government is not prepared to tell the people that it has increased taxes. It is trying to sneak it in. My job as an opposition member is to bring that out. I hope people will remember that, particularly those in the province of Quebec, because they will be hurt. Later in my speech I will point out that if there is a war in the Middle East tomorrow, the people in the Atlantic provinces and Quebec will be the first to be hurt.
Of that $1.67 per gallon, 63 cents goes to the industry, the searchers, producers, refiners, distributors and retailers. They receive 63 cents. The government, which does not do one stitch, not one thing, receives 57 cents, more than twice what the owners receive.

May 13, 1982
Taxation
The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex referred to the United States megaprojects that are being cancelled. The reason is that so much conventional oil has been found. They can cut back their megaprojects because they float. One thing about the Americans, they have the ability to cut and bleed and get on with it. Because of our government trying to solve every problem for every citizen, it does not work in Canada.
I want to make some comments in response to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres). I was astounded at his admission, which was the first I have ever known. He said this is tax by regulation, and the reason is that it gives the government more flexibility to quickly increase taxes. That is exactly what he said. It is true. It gives it the power to increase taxes by a minister signing a piece of paper. Never will those taxes come before this House for review, nor will they therefore, they hope, get out to the Canadian people. Sir, it is a gimmick to avoid facing the people with taxes. When you think about it, the whole purpose of Parliament originally, the entire and sole reason for Parliament, was to control the purse, so that the ruling governments, which in those days were the monarchs, would have to come to the people to get the money.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Quite so.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Well, we are being thrown back in time because the Liberals, for a while at least, are going to avoid it. Then he too went on to imply that the Alberta government had agreed to all the federal taxes. Of course, as I pointed out earlier, that is absolutely untrue. When the Premier of the province of Alberta signed that agreement he was not agreeing to the federal taxes. He was saying in effect that that was their jurisdiction, that "Canadian people will have to deal with the federal government for those taxes, the Alberta people will have to deal with me with respect to the royalty." And he did a good job for the people of Alberta.
The Minister of State for Finance went on to say that the Canadian tax regime is approximately equal to that of other countries, and therefore the Canadian oil companies should be happy. If that were so, Mr. Speaker, why is it that there were some 275 oil rigs leaving this country? If our tax regime is so good and so comparable, why did they leave? It costs hundreds of thousands of dollars to pack up a rig, take it across the border, then get it established, buy more leases, and enter into agreements. It cost a lot of money. Why did they go? The truth is that the tax regimes are not the same.
We have had a substantial change because prior to the National Energy Program, we used to encourage industries, through tax deductions or tax credits, whichever we felt were best, and we would bring in a tax deduction for an oil company doing some work. Any company could therefore go out, do the work and get the benefit of the tax deduction. Now the National Energy Program has changed that. All of the tax money is being collected in Ottawa and the money will then be given out, depending on whether the Liberal government and its bureaucracy decides the company is deserving. What will be the test? The test will be, "Where are you going to drill?"
If you are going to drill in Alberta, you are not going to get very much. If you are going to drill up in the Beaufort on federal land, you are going to get a lot. So taxpayers from the province of Alberta, for example, will be paying tax dollars to Ottawa. If a company wants to work in Alberta, they are not going to get the same grant as would a company going to work on other land, like federal land. That is inherently unfair, because under the tax deduction system the company made the decisions based on where the oil was and where they could get at it. So that is a substantial change, and it will mean less oil production.
The point that is really interesting to me as an Albertan is that prior to the National Energy Program, even though the manufacturing industry in central Canada was having some problems and needed to have federal government help, we had one part of our country that was really going flat out. That was the oil and gas industry in the western basin, moving up into the Arctic and moving off to the offshore on the east coast. That industry was providing tens of thousands of jobs, not for Albertans, Mr. Speaker, because we do not have very many of our own people, but providing jobs for boys and girls from Ontario, Quebec and the rest of the country. We were becoming more unified as a result of that. We were mixing, and it was great.
Now that is all over. As a result of the National Energy Program, the rigs leaving and people not drilling, the Alsands and Cold Lake being cancelled, it is the Ontario young people and the young people from the rest of the country who are now having to go home without a job. The spin-off benefits of the Alsands, where there would be pipe produced in Ontario, equipment and clothes in Quebec, rail cars and pipe in Nova Scotia, are no more. It is not there, Mr. Speaker. Those people are losing their jobs. So it is ironic that, to express a very selfish Albertan point of view, for Alsands not to go on is in the best long-term interests of the people of Alberta. If it is not used by our generation, it will be there for our children, our grandchildren and our great grandchildren. Alberta was prepared to have all of that oil produced. Even with our conventional oil, it would be best if Albertans could leave that in the ground. But they are not doing so, because, in the Canadian dimension, they are producing 1.2 million barrels a day to send it down the pipeline for the rest of Canada. Even at 50 per cent of the world price, that has built up the Alberta heritage trust fund. Alberta could have decided to hold production down, because the Constitution permits that, just export 200,000 barrels a day and keep the remainder for Albertans for the rest of all time. But that is not right. So they built up the heritage trust fund.
That brings me to the next point. The Minister of State for Finance was indicating that Albertans were somehow greedy because they had built up that heritage trust fund. Mr. Speaker, that heritage trust fund has helped the rest of Canadians in several ways. First, it is a source of money that other provinces could come and borrow. It keeps the interest in the country, as
May 13, 1982

against having to go outside the country to borrow the money, which means more dollars flowing out of the country.
Second, several billions of dollars of that heritage trust fund has gone into the Alberta home mortgage corporation, which lends that money out to Alberta citizens to build their homes. That means that there is more CMHC money available for other Canadians. The same occurs with the Agricultural Development Corporation. It uses Alberta heritage trust fund money, and that means that there is more money through the Farm Credit Corporation to other provinces. In that sense, it is a major help. If it were not for the heritage trust fund, more money would have had to flow into Alberta and there would be less available for other provinces.
Then what happens, Mr. Speaker? When Albertans have money, just as when Newfoundlanders have money, they buy a car. Where is the car produced? In Ontario. So you get this tremendous mixing. I was a member of the fiscal tax force and even the four Liberal members sitting on that task force joined us in agreeing unanimously that the Alberta heritage trust fund was in no way a detriment to this country and that the existing economic links would recirculate that money so that we would all benefit a great deal.
Mr. Speaker, I challenge the Minister of State for Finance to rise in his seat and tell me that if the oil and gas were located in Ontario or Quebec, or in both provinces, we would have the same National Energy Program. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, there is not one way that one of those members opposite can stand and honestly say that if the oil and gas were in Ontario and Quebec we would have the same National Energy Program. Their people would not permit it. The only way they can get away with it is that it is in the west, in Alberta, with only 21 members, and while we stand here and try to explain to them the problems it is causing, it does not affect them because they do not have their own constituents there. That was true at least until a while ago. I think their constituents are going there now. The young men and the young women who went west to get jobs found no jobs there. I hope they are in yelling and screaming, because it is just not right. It should not be. If members opposite want to come with me, I will take you out and I will introduce you to people who have lost their jobs, to men and women who have put 20 and 30 years of their lives in building up a small business, only to have it smashed. Those are human beings, Mr. Speaker. Those are hot, living bodies out there that have lost it. They would not have lost it, if it were not for the National Energy Program.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Right on. All we have is empty seats on the other side.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what have we got? Canadians need to know exactly what the government has done. In fact, this bill tonight contains three new taxes, but it is part of seven taxes that are increasing the burden of Canadians at the grassroots level. These are regressive taxes which are being levied on people. We have the PGRT, the IORT, the NGGLT, the COC, the PCC, an excise tax and a sales tax. There are seven
Taxation
individual and separate taxes which are coming out of the pockets of Canadians directly.
The whole National Energy Program is based on a false model designed by intellects who have never had to meet a payroll in their entire lives. The officials in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, and the minister himself, have never gone out and operated a business. They have never set up a business. They have never had to hire people. They have never had to produce. They have never had to pay people at the end of the month. They have never had to pay workmen's compensation premiums or unemployment insurance premiums. They have never had to make income tax deductions and Canada Pension Plan deductions. They have never had to stay up until midnight filling out their own papers. They are indulging in an academic, intellectual exercise. At will, by signing a paper, they can increase the workload of people in the field.
While it saddens me that Canadians have to do this, I am pleased they are starting to fight back, and they are fighting back in several ways. They turfed out a government which believed government should take everything unto itself. They turfed out the government in Saskatchewan. That government was buying land from people and denying them the right to own property. That government was nationalizing and creating Crown corporations. That government was into every conceivable type of business but still taxing the people because Crown corporations did not have to say they were sorry and therefore kept coming back to the Saskatchewan provincial purse. The government kept kicking in tax dollars until finally people said, "Enough".
When I was in Saskatchewan and knocked on doors for three days during the election campaign, it was a genuine pleasure to hear people say, "We have had enough." They wanted to turf the government out, and they did.
Canadians are beginning to rebel in another way, and I think that is just great because the ultimate way to stop a government is to stop the flow of tax dollars. Hon. members will have noticed that the underground economy is expanding enormously. At a time when we do not really need much cash because there are so many credit cards-and they are used- the use of cash in our society is growing enormously. The reason is that people want to be paid in cash because in an underground economy no taxes are paid. While that is unfair in the sense that other people are paying their taxes, it is a sign that people are waking up and saying "No". Rather than doing that, I encourage people to wait until the next election and put in a party and a government which would not take everything away from them.
As hon. members have heard me say previously, a slave is simply someone who is taxed 100 per cent in the sense that someone else makes decisions as to the human rights of that slave, where he lives, where he works and where he sleeps. As an economic creature, a slave is simply taxed 100 per cent. All that person's economic rent goes into the hands of someone

May 13, 1982
Taxation
else who decides how it is spent. That is exactly where we are because when we add up our municipal taxes, our provincial taxes and our federal taxes, we find that over 55 per cent of the sweat of our brows goes into the hands of someone else who decides how to spend it. That is the major difference between the parties in this House. The party to the left, the NDP, clearly would tax away 80 per cent or 90 per cent, as is done in the socialist countries of Sweden and the United Kingdom. In places like Russia and China 100 per cent is taxed away. Hon. members opposite in the Liberal Party now believe in the same thing. They want to take away so that they can pay back in the form of grants. This party would not do that, and this party will be a real alternative in the next election.
This bill deals with the goals of the National Energy Program. First, the bill deals with self-sufficiency. That goal has been lost, and that is a tragedy because Canada continues to use about 1.7 to 1.8 million barrels of oil a day. We were getting about 1.2 million barrels a day of Alberta light crude, and we were getting about 200,000 barrels of synthetic crude per day from Alberta's tar sands. We were importing about
400,000	to 450,000 barrels a day. We are still faced with the reality of importing 400,000 to 450,000 barrels a day and, if there is ever trouble in the Middle East, that supply will be cut off and we will be exactly where we were in 1978 during the last Middle East crisis when suddenly we realized we were exposed. When the OPEC increased the price, we were caught. We had no choice but to pay the price. If we were self-sufficient, we would not give a hoot what the rest of the world does. If the OPEC were to put its price up to $500 a barrel and if we were self-sufficient, we would decide how much we would pay in the Canadian interest.
But we are not there. We are still importing, and that is how we are getting ourselves into a real jam. If there is a war tomorrow, the people in the Atlantic provinces and Quebec will be cold. They will be cold because we will not be able to get oil to them.
Alberta's offer was incredibly generous. What Alberta said then was: "Pay us, as owners, up to 85 per cent of the world price, and we will guarantee that with that money we will put those tar sands plants in." As our conventional crude supplies dropped, as they are dropping even this year, Alberta would have guaranteed there would be synthetic oil in production to offset that, as well as to cover imported oil. Alberta also guaranteed that the extra money would be used in Manitoba to develop the hydroelectric project on the Nelson. Alberta guaranteed it would go into Quebec and Newfoundland to develop their water resources in the north so that we could be self-sufficient in all forms of energy. Well, that is gone, and it is a tragedy because it need not be gone. We as Canadians could be self-sufficient, and should not have to be beholden to anyone. No form of blackmail should get us.
The next goal of the National Energy Program was Canadi-anization. When the Liberal government, now in its socialist form, talks about Canadianization, Canadians should never be fooled because the government is not giving Canadians a chance to buy shares. Indeed, it is expropriating shares from
Canadian citizens. Many Canadians held shares in Petrofina. Those shares were expropriated. Many Canadians held shares in Altantic Richfield. They were expropriated. Many Canadians owned shares in Pacific Petroleums. They were expropriated. The Liberal-NDP coalition kept the right of property out of the Constitution because if we had the constitutionally entrenched right to ownership of property-and that includes shares-the government could not under the Canada Business Corporations Act, expropriate our shares because the clauses of the Canada Business Corporations Act dealing with that would be null and void. The government would have to buy my shares. It would have to negotiate with me. If it gave me enough money, of course I would sell, but the government could not take my shares away. We do not have the right to own property because that would block nationalization.
The Liberals agreed on a Friday to include the right to own property. The next day the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) held a press conference and told the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that if he continued to propose the inclusion of the right to own property in the charter, the NDP would withdraw its support. The Liberals came crawling back on the Monday following. Having agreed to include the right to own property on the Friday, the Liberals withdrew that right and used their majority. In the next election campaign there will be a plank in my party's election platform proposing to give the people that right, and then they will truly have that right.
What has been the effect of his great Canadianization? Let me give exact figures. They are truly astounding. The amount of money which has left this country to purchase the shares of foreign-owned companies is $5.3 billion, the amount which has left this country by way of take-over when Canadian companies have borrowed money in the United States, primarily to buy other companies, was $4.9 billion. Then there was an unidentified outflow of some $8.4 billion, for a total cash out flow of $18.6 billion. Let me tell hon. members why $10 billion went out. We had foreign ownership of shares. The cost of those shares was a dividend, the long-term average of those dividends was 3 per cent to 5 per cent. It must be remembered that a dividend is only paid if a company is making profit. In good years you would lose the dividend and in bad years the dividend would stay because one would not be declared. What we have effectively done with $10 billion is to convert that from foreign equity ownership into foreign debt, on which we pay between 15 per cent and 20 per cent. So whether it is a good year or a bad year, 15 per cent to 20 per cent of that $10 billion goes out just to service it. That does not count the $10 billion for the principal, and that is the tragedy.
We have already been through this during the 1920s and even before, when most of Canada's foreign ownership was in the form of debt. A great intellectual exercise went on at that time when the bright boys of the day decided that because the interest flows out in good years and in bad years, the debt had to be converted into foreign equity, and then a dividend would
May 13, 1982

just be paid in the good years. That is why we have foreign ownership today. Now we are doing exactly the opposite and turning it back into foreign debt and facing that hemorrhage of money.
There is another figure that must be considered, Mr. Speaker. At the present time $31.4 billion short-term speculative money flows into Canada. That is the international, Arab, petroleum, energy money-the petro-dollars, the international banking community money. It is the capital market that flows wherever the investment is best. In order to keep that money here and to protect our dollar, we have had to increase our interest rates to 15 per cent or 20 per cent. That is why Canadians are hurting today, Mr. Speaker. We lost all our direct investment money, $18 billion of it, and we have had to bring in $31 billion of speculative money.
That money would be gone by noon tomorrow if some other country offered an extra 2 per cent interest. That would justify cost and we would be left holding the bag. That is why we are forced to keep our interest rates up. It is not because of anything that the people of Canada have done wrong; it is something that the government has done to them. People should remember that is was done by a Liberal government.
I could go on for a long time talking about this, Mr. Speaker, and 1 could deal with the comments of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). EMERGENCY MEASURES-ORDER IN COUNCIL PROVISIONS AFFECTING MANPOWER. (B) EFFECT ON UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will know that for some time now I have been exploring the implications of the emergency planning orders as documented in The Canada Gazette of June 10, 1981. Among other things, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is empowered in peacetime to nationalize the energy industry in Canada. The minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) is empowered to nationalize the means of production in Canada. These immense powers given to various cabinet ministers are of growing concern to me and, according to my mail and that of many other members, to Canadians all across the country. That is why ten days ago I rose to ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) questions regarding the implications that order had for his portfolio, and therefore all Canadians. As I pointed out at the time, he is empowered to, "establish a population register for the effective management of manpower and arrange any required international manpower transaction." I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that those are peacetime powers being given to the minister under a very loose definition of what constitutes an emergency. In answering my question, if you can call it an answer, the minister said:
-that any time there is a major catastrophe that would affect this country, there are obviously international implications in terms of the movement of workers and movement of people across borders.
May 13, 1982

I ask, Mr. Speaker, what constitutes a national emergency which would have those broad international implications? Suppose there were large scale floods. Is that big enough to call for an international transfer of manpower? Suppose there were an earthquake of massive dimensions in Canada. Should that empower the minister to register all manpower in Canada and transfer them to other sovereign countries in the world? Suppose there were a drought for several years in Canada as we experienced it in the 1930s. Is that enough of a catastrophe to justify empowering the minister to register everyone in Canada and then ship them out of the country? The specific question is: what kind of an excuse does the minister need? Under what circumstances does a domestic national emergency call for the Minister of Employment and Immigration to transfer Canadians to another country? These are the bizarre implications of the emergency planning order.
When the Solidarity union in Poland faced military rule, and in fact the entire country was under military rule, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that the demands of Polish workers were "excessive". I came across a quotation in the Solidarity union weekly newspaper which I should like to read. It indicated what might transpire as follows:
Militarization of work enterprises which converts bureaucratic directives into commands; military courts replace civil courts; all union activities as well as activities by other organizations and associations are terminated; all public gatherings outside of religious observances are outlawed; the censorship law is suspended, which means a position of arbitrary censorship could include the proscription of any publication; limitation on freedom of travel out of the country as well as-attention-movement within the country.
This was published by Solidarity workers two days before the imposition of martial law in Poland.
Several months ago in committee I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) whether a general strike would be enough to impose the emergency planning order in Canada. He said, "If it got serious enough, yes." That is an implication of bizarre proportions. On that same day I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) whether, according to the emergency planning order, he was able to regulate and control conditions of work, rates of remuneration, and occupational safety. Again, this is a peacetime power, and the Minister of Labour is able to abrogate all union contracts and is able to deny workers the legitimacy of union agreements which have been arrived at. I want to point out that the powers given to the Minister of Labour under peacetime are nothing short of dictatorial. At the time the Minister of Labour gave an even more alarming answer. He said:
Until that emergency situation appears on the horizon, the integrity of collective agreements will prevail.
What does he mean?

Mr. Speaker, we all know the interest taken by the honourable member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr.Friesen) in the issue of emergency measures. It must be said however that, by itself, the emergency planning order gives the minister no authority to establish a population register nor arrange any emergency international manpower transactions. Those are the responsibilities of the national emergency manpower administration that can only be formally established in cases of serious national emergencies. And even then, the enactment of such an emergency act remains a prerequisite.
Section 5 of the order only requires the minister to develop and update appropriate plans and duties for the establishment and operation of the above-mentioned administration. It does not empower him to exercise responsibilities, powers and functions mentioned in the appendix to the order. The same goes for labour conditions, pay rates, work safety and labour relations, that would be the responsibility of the above-mentioned administration.

AIRPORTS-(A) POSSIBLE CHANGE IN STATUS OF DORVAL AND MIRABEL AIRPORTS-(B) REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT EXAMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the answer he gave yesterday to my question dealing with a possible transfer of services from Dorval to Mirabel, which was directed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), and in which I asked for a genuine consultation process with all the interested parties, namely the air transport industry, labour, Montreal businessmen and above all the public, the minister answered, and I quote:
It may well be that we shall have a public process of consultation on the decision I shall recommend to cabinet, but the decision has not yet been made.
If I read his answer correctly, this means he will first make a decision, then a recommendation to cabinet, and after that we might have that public consultation process.
This is just not good enough. What kind of a democracy are we living in when the minister, in a matter which is as important as this to a population of some two million people, is beating around the bush with regard to the question of a full public consultation with the air industry, businessmen of Montreal, the travelling public and the unions who represent the workers who may have to move from Dorval eventually? What is the problem with a consultation process? Is it because the department is afraid to have a full public consultation process? Are they are afraid of the facts?
I am absolutely amazed that we are faced with the situation where several options are being presented to the public while

May 13, 1982
Adjournment Debate
another one is being presented to a particular segment of the public. They are the 33 mayors from the north side of Montreal who, as well as members on this side who are supporting that Mirabel effort, have legitimate local interests. However, that local interest is certainly not anywhere near as important as the more general interest which exists on the part of the vast majority of the people living on the island of Montreal and on the south shore opposite Montreal in the continuing full use of Dorval airport for domestic and North American service.
Under the circumstances, we are finding that the options that are being presented are limited. The two most important options are not even being considered. Those two options are the status quo or the closing of Mirabel altogether. If options are going to be considered, these latter two are legitimate and must be considered and be part of any public consultation process.
Finally, I think we should review the history of Mirabel for a moment. I was aware of and supportive of the political reasons for the construction of Mirabel airport in the first place. There were technological reasons advanced for it at that time: noise reduction and the argument that Mirabel would be the gateway for freight transfer and passenger transfer to the rest of North America. Technological developments have bypassed Mirabel. Sound has been reduced by two thirds, and aircraft can now fly almost twice as far. Therefore, flights from Europe can go to the centre of North America or even the North American west coast. The dream of Mirabel as a gateway to North America has gone forever.
The present reality is something quite different. Mirabel is there and we are losing in the order of $25 million a year in operating costs. That is regrettable. If we want to be totally hardnosed, I guess we should shut Mirabel down. At the moment I think we can consider leaving it open, hopefully, because the present passenger traffic, something which not even the so-called experts in the department could have predicted, will increase. However, I doubt that it will happen to the point where it would justify the full use of Mirabel.
We are now in a situation where it has been suggested that we replace the present $25 million operating loss with an expenditure of some $400 million at least, $200 million from the public sector and another $175 million or so from the private sector. The interest on that alone is two or three times the present operating costs of Mirabel.
There are other items here that we have to mention. The travelling public in Montreal certainly do not want the move. Business in Montreal certainly does not want the move. Twenty minutes may seem a minor amount of time to a lot of people, but it is just enough time, 20 minutes each way, to make many businessmen and the travelling public decide to take a plane to Toronto and make a transfer there, or to take a plane into the United States and make their transfer somewhere further down the line rather than to spend extra money
themselves on gasoline or on a $40 taxi trip. If the recommendation that the northern mayors are making is followed through, the end result will be a decrease in total passenger traffic coming through the combination of Mirabel and Dorval.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AIRPORTS-(A) POSSIBLE CHANGE IN STATUS OF DORVAL AND MIRABEL AIRPORTS-(B) REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT EXAMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is apparent to anyone who has followed the recent events and has read Hansard that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is giving the Mirabel-Dorval issue his fullest attention. The solution must be one that is reached after a full examination of the long-term development needs of the Montreal area. Information provided to this House as recently as during the debate this afternoon has shown that there have been many reviews and opinions on this extremely complex and difficult issue. With the release of the interim report on airport role options in February, 1981, known as phase one, all interested parties were invited to submit comments and concerns on two proposed options, with a view to providing broader input to phase two, which is the detailed cost benefit and arrangements of these options. This indication represents a genuine public process of consultation as called for by the hon. member, but the process of consultation has gone farther than this.
The hon. member will recall that the minister has personally met with large delegations representing both the Dorval and Mirabel areas. He has also personally met with the president of Air Canada and CP Air to discuss the issue, as was recently disclosed in an article in the Montreal Gazette. So there can be no doubt that the minister is taking the issue seriously and has made considerable efforts to hear the interested parties. The minister is searching for the best possible solution. It may be that the solution will not satisfy everyone, but the hon. member can be assured that once the minister is satisfied that every aspect has been fully considered, he will not hesitate to recommend a course of action to his colleagues, however difficult it may be.

subtopic: FINANCE-REQUEST FOR INCREASED TAX REBATE ON FARM FUEL
FINANCE-REQUEST FOR INCREASED TAX REBATE ON FARM FUEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 8 I raised a question with the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) concerning the rebate on farm fuels. The reason I raised it was that 1 believe everyone knows that there is much difficulty, not only in farming communities, but also in the business community as a whole across the country. Specifically, in relation to the farming community, it is very important that we maintain a productive agricultural economy at home so that we can have access to relatively inexpensive food and so that we can meet what most people believe to be an expanding export market for our agricultural products. If we are to do those two things, we must ensure that farmers stay in production.
In the farming community, we have been experiencing some very large increases in the cost of farming, and it looks as though this will continue. As we all know, farming has become very capital intensive because farmers spend much money on
May 13, 1982

machinery and other costs, such as fuels, fertilizers, insecticides and pesticides, most of which are based on the petroleum industry.
Therefore, I specifically requested the minister to take a look at the taxes which are being collected simply on farm fuels, not on fertilizers made from petroleum products and not on insecticides and pesticides.
I see the parliamentary secretary is here this evening. He will know that approximately 40 per cent of the cost of farm fuels is made up of federal excise tax. It is presently about 40 cents a gallon on diesel fuel and 60 cents a gallon on gasoline. That is an alarming amount of money. The sad part is that that amount of money which the federal government collects from farmers in the form of taxes on farm fuel will increase.
I have some figures which my colleague, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), used in his speech this evening which point this out. In 1980, the cost on an average size farm in western Canada, a thousand acres, related to all petroleum products such as motor fuel, heating fuel and fertilizer, was estimated to be $11,800. In 1981 it was estimated at $16,750. the disconcerting figure is that the projected 1986 figure is $42,000. The tax on farm fuels is expected to go to almost half that, $16,800 for an average thousand acre farm. If that happens, farmers will have a very bad time trying to stay in business. The farm community will have a bad time meeting export commitments. We all know that a healthy agricultural economy adds to the domestic economy.
Despite the fact that we import a lot of food out of season, citrus fruits from the southern United States and all kinds of other foods that we cannot grow in this country because of our climate, when you compare our agricultural exports with what we bring in in the form of imports, you find that there is still a surplus of approximately $3 billion.
Canadian agriculture is thus a very large earner of foreign exchange. Therefore, it should be very important to this government to keep that industry healthy. It will not stay healthy if the federal government chooses to tax it out of business. I submit very sincerely that we are coming very close to that point.
The government should look at what it is doing to the farm community in terms of taxes. If through excess taxes we drive farmers out of business, and therefore have less food available domestically, the consumer will have to pay more. This will not only add to inflation but cause all other kinds of problems. The distinguished chairman of our agriculture committee, who is sitting beside the parliamentary secretary, will understand that a very efficient agricultural industry at home is important not only for our exports, but to maintain a healthy and productive economy at home.
I know that when the parliamentary secretary responds with an answer prepared for him by the department, he will state that any remission of taxes will add to the deficit and that the opposition is being inconsistent by screaming at the government to hold down expenses while at the same time proposing measures that will add to the deficit.
Adjournment Debate
Let me point out that farmers who go out of business do not pay taxes. They will require some form of social assistance and that will add to the deficit. They not only lose the job they created for themselves, but in many cases lose the opportunity to make jobs for others they employ.
Farmers who go out of business do not buy machinery. That hurts central Canada where a lot of the manufacturing takes place. We have seen evidence of that in the House. Massey-Ferguson, White Farm Equipment and International Harvester, which has a big plant in Hamilton, are all in trouble. When those equipment manufacturers are out of business or are suffering financial hardship as a result of farmers not buying their products, they do not pay taxes, and that adds to the deficit.
The government should take a close look at what the opposition is suggesting in the terms of an increase in the rebate on farm fuels. When the federal government is taking, as I said, approximately 40 cents a gallon on diesel fuel and 60 cents a gallon on gasoline, and the rebate is 7 cents a gallon, if farmers and businessmen apply for that rebate, there would be nothing wrong with increasing that, doubling it or tripling it, particularly when you look at what is going to happen as the National Energy Program and the pricing agreement reached with the producing provinces last September comes into effect. A $42,000 tax bill on a thousand acre farm means $40 an acre tax on farmland. I do not know how you can expect farmers to stay in business, to be efficient, to provide food for our consumers at home, and at the same time to look after what we believe our obligation is to the international community, to feed them, while at the same time, helping out our balance of payments.
I would hope that when the parliamentary secretary rises this evening to answer my question, he will take into consideration what the opposition is suggesting.

speakeroldname: Mr. Remi Bujold (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: FINANCE-REQUEST FOR INCREASED TAX REBATE ON FARM FUEL
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) has expressed his concern about farm fuel costs and has requested that the present tax be increased.
The government recognizes that all Canadians are experiencing increased costs in a number of areas. All householders have to pay more for food, heating fuel and electricity. All persons who operate motor vehicles or equipment powered with internal combustion engines are experiencing cost increases, both because fuel is more expensive and because the costs of repair labour and repair parts have increased.
The government has mitigated the cost of gasoline for commercial users by rebating 100 per cent of the seven cents a gallon special excise tax which is imposed on all gasoline for use in internal combustion engines. Farmers are, of course,

May 13, 1982
Adjournment Debate
entitled to receive this rebate when the gasoline is used in their farming activities.
The special excise tax is also rebated to municipalities, provincial government departments, clergymen, the handicapped, transportation companies and a number of other users.
Increasing the rebate to farmers beyond the amount of excise tax originally paid, would constitute a special subsidy to members of the farming community. I believe it would be difficult to single out farmers as being more deserving of a special subsidy than, for example, loggers, commercial fishermen, municipal transit systems, taxi operators, freight forwarders and the handicapped, as all of these users face the problems identified by the hon. member.
Proceeding in that manner would cause a substantial loss to the treasury and further increase the deficit. In the light of this fact, it would be difficult for the government to proceed as the member for Portage-Marquette has suggested. Even though farm fuel costs are rising, the cost of fuel is generally lower in Canada than in most other countries around the world. In some countries internal combustion fuel costs are more than double the costs being experienced in Canada, and those countries impose heavy tax levies on those prices as well.
